#110054. 10 Best Coffee Table Books to Buy in 2026, According to AD

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2744 w)

10 Best Coffee Table Books to Buy in 2026, According to AD

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2744 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whether placed on a shelf or the coffee table in your living room, coffee table books can easily serve as pieces of decor.
  • We’ve picked the best coffee table books from this year’s batch, and we’re thrilled to hole up with them until warmer days make their appearance.
  • According to recent reports, there are over 400 pages of inspiration-packed interiors to peruse in Amy Astley’s second coffee table book, AD at Home.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whether placed on a shelf or the coffee table in your living room, coffee table books can easily serve as pieces of decor. “I feel that books complete any room,” indicates global editorial director Amy Astley. “They are a record of your life and passions—I am profoundly connected to all of my printed matter!”.

We’ve picked the best coffee table books from this year’s batch, and we’re thrilled to hole up with them until warmer days make their appearance. Here are our favorites from 2026’s bountiful assortment of debuts—many of them featuring AD-approved talents—all packed with invaluable design insights and gorgeous interiors past and present.

According to recent reports, there are over 400 pages of inspiration-packed interiors to peruse in Amy Astley’s second coffee table book, AD at Home. Throughout the book you’ll find dreamy pictures and thoughtful essays pulled straight from our pages, including anecdotes from former cover stars like Marc Jacobs, Dakota Johnson, Gwyneth Paltrow, and more. “Even in a world of oversharing on social media, there is still such a frisson of entree in glimpsing the private world of a public figure, and AD will eternally share the fantasy,” Astley says in her editor’s letter. With the holidays approaching, we think AD at Home also makes a perfect gift for the collector, the design enthusiast, and anyone who’s just a little bit nosy about what’s going on behind a celebrity’s closed doors.

Recent findings suggest that created by AD France’s former editor-in-chief, Marie Kalt, La Bibliothèque de l’Amateur is a collection of compact, accessible monographs devoted to the great names of 20th-century design. The contents explore the work of acclaimed designers, including Alvar Aalto, Charlotte Perriand, Ettore Sottsass, while including emerging talents in the conversation as well. Each $30 volume pairs a brief introduction with about 60 images and detailed captions, offering an engaging visual primer on a designer’s life and work.

In a recent development, global features director Sam Cochran’s debut coffee table book opens with the words, “Nothing is interesting unless it is personal.” His project, American Designers at Home, brings that idea to life beautifully. The volume takes you inside the homes of 20 leading designers across the country—including Andre Mellone, Kelly Wearstler, and Robin Standefer and Stephen Alesch of Roman and Williams—each reflecting its creator’s distinctive taste and personal passions. “As my dear friend Markham Roberts—one of the designers featured in the book—says, ‘If stuff makes you happy, you want it around,’ and this book makes me very happy,” says global interiors and garden director Alison Levasseur.

Levasseur claims that Simon Upton’s most recent release with Rizzoli contains “beauty and poetry on every page.” The title is a nod to the iconic London A–Z: The detailed street atlas that every Londoner seemed to own in the 1980s and early 2000s, pre-Google Maps. Like its namesake, Upton’s book is an expert guide, specifically to a world of extraordinary interiors and visual pleasures. “Some of my favorite stories ever to appear in the pages of AD were photographed by Upton,” says Levasseur. “Many are gathered here, including those featuring Adwoa Aboah, Dakota Johnson, and Sienna Miller.”.

This beautiful debut monograph not only showcases Chicago architect Joan Craig's elegant classical architecture, but it also spotlights the artistry behind it. “I love that Craig shares the spotlight with the often-unsung craftspeople who bring her interiors to life, including Brittany’s masters of straw marquetry and Bologna’s terrazzo artisans,” states senior digital editor Catherine Hong. “It's a tribute to design excellence and also the art of collaboration.".

In a recent development, “Whether or not you’d ever dare to decorate with Sasha Bikoff’s over-the-top flair, this book is guaranteed to make a splash on your coffee table,” indicates Hong. Behind its trippy, hot-pink cover lies screaming color, clashing eras, and utter fantasy. The designer lives by her “Rule of Three Wows”—chronicled in the pages—and her book is, accordingly, loud, wildly fun, and a little bit insane in the best way.

Studio Valle de Valle’s debut monograph offers a refined window into the AD100 firm’s singular vision and creative evolution—surveying 10 projects from the past 10 years. Printed in Italy, with photography by Stephen Kent Johnson, the pages demonstrate the firm’s interior philosophy of creating spaces that feel personal, layered, and deeply inhabitable. “The edition isn’t just a tour de visual force, it’s an art object unto itself,” says Cochran. “I would expect nothing less from these brilliant auteurs.".

Industry observers note that “One of Meyer Davis’s greatest strengths is how cofounders Will Meyer and Gray Davis distill references, ideas, and desires into a highly refined vision,” notes AD PRO senior editor Mel Studach. As client Jenna Lyons puts it in the book’s foreword, “They gave me clarity.” Beyond a printed body of work, The Language of Home is a testament to the collaborations that shape the studio's warm, reductive interiors. Designed with honest materials and a contemporary lens, the featured residences—a modern glass house in the Berkshires and an earthen dwelling in Puerto Escondido—reflect their inhabitants with a calm, clear ease.

The inaugural monograph from AD100 design duo Humbert & Poyet showcases their signature brand of eclectic French luxury, blending Art Deco glamour, midcentury modernism, and the decorative arts. Spanning residential and hospitality projects around the world, the book by AD contributing editor Gay Gassmann takes readers from a French Riviera villa to a Milan restaurant housed in a 17th-century chapel, with stops in Upcoming York, Paris, Monaco, and Seoul.

In Upcoming York: Atelier AM, Alexandra and Michael Misczynkski, the married couple behind the AD100 firm, shine a light on their New York projects, all beautifully captured by François Halard. Spotlighting a range of projects like elegant Manhattan residences and more relaxed Long Island retreats, contributor Ingrid Abramovitch says the book itself is “equally exquisite, with a cover resembling wood grain, and high-gloss pages printed in Italy.”.

Industry observers note that 2026 AD Latest American Voices honoree Amber Guyton first burst onto the design scene by way of her hit blog, Blessed Little Bungalow. “Her debut book brings the same wit and spirit to the printed page in a kaleidoscope of color and pattern,” says Cochran. Senior shopping editor Nashia Baker adds that the pages “truly embody how to bring personality to any room.” Throughout the book, she makes a case for maximalism, and distills her approach into four pillars: joy, culture, layers, and intention.

“This book is perfect for cinephiles, design-lovers, or anyone with a case of wanderlust,” claims senior digital editor Rachel Wallace. Film is one way to travel the world without ever leaving the sofa, and with her new project On Location, longtime AD contributor Cathy Whitlock takes readers on a global cinematic journey. The book goes behind the scenes of films that make you want to hop on a flight and never look back. Colorful Mexico City scenes from Frida and Marie Antoinette’s famous Palace of Versailles shooting location are both represented.

Organized by a series of chapter essays rather than specific projects, AD100 designer Dan Fink’s debut book explores bigger questions on how spaces, objects, and compositions move us across time. At the same time, the book spotlights several career-defining projects from his namesake studio, including previously unpublished interiors like Manhattan penthouses, Hawaiian beach retreats, Hollywood homes, and more.

Industry observers note that one of the few completely fail-proof gifts is one of the best coffee table books of the season—weighty tomes whose thick, glossy pages feature stunning photographs and illustrations, to be specific. On a superficial level, they add ambiance, whether you place them in a library or a living room. But the best ones live in your home forever, while expanding your horizons far beyond. They also come across as far more memorable and thoughtful than the expected candle or bottle of champagne. Like works of fiction, there are limitless topics that can make deciding on an eye-catching hardcover (that doubles as home decor) seemingly impossible.

But that’s where we come in. Our team has gathered its favorite giftable recommendations for everyone from tennis enthusiasts to globe-trotters to interior design aficionados. From a book focused on hotels around the world to another that spotlights Tokyo style, there are plenty of ways to adorn the coffee tables of all the people on your holiday gift list. Most of them came out in 2024, but we’ve also included a few evergreen picks that make worthy gifts any year.

Plus, if you’re down to the wire on last-minute gifts, rest assured that most of these selections are available (and even marked down ahead of the holidays!) on Amazon.

In a recent development, après-ski style needs no introduction in a season full of fuzzy Fair Isle sweaters, but it’s the cozy interiors of the chalets along the world’s most popular ski slopes that are worthy of a second look. From the wooden beams of an A-frame to the blazing fireplaces set within them, AD contributor Kathryn O’Shea-Evans pores over the finer details in this fun, wintery escape.

As associate digital editor Maya Ibbitson previously described it, “Alpine Style is a true compendium of resort luxury,” spanning spectacular chalets from Gstaad to Aspen and featuring the works of AD PRO Directory members such as Massucco Warner, Robbins Architecture, and Kara Adam Interiors.

Japan’s interiors are a perpetual reference for modern-day designers, and whether you’re a proponent of wabi-sabi principles or just looking for small space ideas, Tokyo Style will help you explore both.

Originally published in 1993, it’s since become a collector’s item and cult classic, and it was recommended by commerce writer Julia Harrison for anyone who would appreciate a more intimate glimpse of Tokyo’s dwellings: “Apartamento, an imprint that consistently delivers on elite design, has reintroduced Tsuzuki’s collection for us to enjoy in its full brilliance—that is, not a ‘fine’ condition original at $170 with $90 shipping from eBay.”.

Prefaced with a foreword by Spike Lee, BLK MKT Vintage peers into the world of the Brooklyn antique shop’s endlessly curious founders Jannah Handy and Kiyanna Stewart. “This monograph teems with more than 300 studies of vintage ephemera and reads like a collage with context, or an I spy for your inner adult archivist,” writes Ibbitson of the book. For collectors, Sydney Gore pinpoints it as a must-have for your rotation.

Donald Judd’s considered, minimalist approach to design has fostered its own cult of acolytes who, these days, emulate his daybeds and chairs on Instagram.

It has been revealed that for the true Juddheads, the Judd Foundation has produced a new book edited by his children Rainer and Flavin Judd that chronicles more than one hundred of his functional works produced between 1970 and 1992. “Mixed in are the juiciest bits: photos from past and present of those pieces in Judd-designed spaces in New York and Marfa,” Ibbitson writes.

AD’s Milan correspondent Laura May Todd penned a delightful homage to Italian living this year, one which spans from historic palaces in Venice to the homes of creatives like Luca Guadagnino along with midcentury Milanese apartments, so you can enjoy a small taste of la dolce vita on each page.

It was one of the AD PRO team’s favorite book releases this fall, one which should suit the person on your list who never got over their Italian study abroad or is manifesting a Sicilian villa in their future.

For the person on your list who delights in having people over, How They Entertain, released this fall, serves as a comprehensive guide to (and celebration of) the art of hosting.

Written by Pierre Sauvage, it’s chock-full of inspiration for your next dinner party, from recipes to design notes on arranging a tabletop to remember, as well as interviews with tastemakers like Laura Gonzalez about their particular philosophy on entertaining guests.

Considering this year’s smash summer hit Challengers and the enduring popularity of tenniscore (polos, skorts, and all), it’s clear that tennis is a lifestyle that has captured the imagination of many people, avid tennis players or not.

This book recommended by the AD PRO team earlier this year is dedicated to a more, uh, underserved cross section of the sport: the backdrops where athletes volley their way to tournament glory (clay, grass, asphalt, and beyond) in locales from Queens to Kenya.

AD100 designer Jeremiah Brent is no stranger to the pages of this very magazine, and his new book is a friends and family affair studded with stars, like Oprah and legendary choreographer Fatima Robinson, with whom Brent has formed close connections over the past 20 years.

We’ve previously described the book (layered with sentimental photos and newly introduced snapshots of contributors in their home) as “more scrapbook than design manifesto, a love letter to the spaces that people have inhabited and inherited over the years.” Read AD’s extensive interview with Brent for more backstory behind (and tidbits from) the book.

In a recent development, for art buffs with a fondness for the Harlem Renaissance—an era synonymous with greats like Aaron Douglas, known as the father of African-American art—this upcoming book compiled by MoMA curator Denise Murrell is an excellent title to know. “Having this book is about as close as you’ll ever get to owning one of the original masterpieces featured in the Harlem Renaissance exhibition at The Met,” Gore states.

Self-interested plug here, but we really couldn’t publish a guide to coffee table books without mentioning our own, AD at 100: A Century of Style. For the design buff with an appetite for lush interiors and a healthy curiosity for how A-listers live, there’s no more satisfying holiday treat than this tome that delves into the homes of the Obamas, David Hockney, Diana Vreeland, and beyond. It also serves as a bird’s eye view of a century in design and architecture, including the works of Frank Gehry, David Hicks, Frank Lloyd Wright, and much, much more.

Architecture has a reputation for myopia when it comes to its foremost voices, but this book seeks to rectify the past with a fresh overview of some of its most brilliant underrepresented talents, including interviews with female architects around the globe such as Tatiana Bilbao, Liz Diller, and Julia Gamolina.

“100 Women offers a refreshing reframe of the built environment outside of the male-dominated Western canon, proving the benefits of sourcing alternative points of reference,” Ibbitson wrote of it in AD PRO’s guide to the best new design books out this past spring.

Colony founder Jean Lin has mentored and platformed some of the design world’s brightest rising stars, and in her first book out this year, she tapped a wide pool of creatives to explore the concept of collections that inform their work, from ceramicist Stephanie H. Shih’s cache of soy sauce bottles to Mira Nakashima’s stockpile of lumber inherited from her father, architect turned furniture maker George Nakashima.

That’s just one facet of the book Ibbitson previously described as an “encyclopedic, elemental study of artist studios, profiles, materials, and everything else under the design umbrella,” with plenty of wisdom imparted within its pages, from how-tos to styling tips. Read our interview with Lin for more of her notes on curating a collection of your own.

Luna Luna—a 1980s artist-led amusement park featuring works by icons of the art world such as Jean-Michel Basquiat, Keith Haring, Salvador Dalí, and David Hockney—is experiencing a resurgence as of late, what with a newly introduced retrospective at The Shed this year, along with a revival of the park itself in Los Angeles late last year.

Sources indicate that this 2023 book takes a deeper dive into Luna Luna’s history blending fine art with the playful energy of a carnival—encompassing rides, interactive installations, and surreal sculptures. It comes recommended by associate visuals editor Shani Kravetz, who nods to the book’s breadth of archival media within, from photos to sketches, that are accompanied by behind-the-scenes stories.

For jet-setters who love to live large on vacation, Spencer Bailey’s Design: The Leading Hotels of the World (released just this month) is one sure way to sustain a sense of wanderlust. His latest book takes readers on a visual journey to 80 countries around the globe, inviting them to mentally book into sumptuous spaces from The Okura in Tokyo to the Portrait Hotel in Milan. It’s rounded out by notable travel and design writers like Maria Cristina Didero and Mark Ellwood, who lend us their travel tips, on top of their reflections on the lodgings featured within.

Hyundai is overhauling the Kona, and it looks like it may still be offered as an EV after all

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (545 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hyundai is skipping the typical mid-cycle refresh and plans to launch a completely redesigned Kona, with a sleek new style and an updated high-tech interior.
  • It’s been nearly four years since Hyundai introduced the second-generation Kona, meaning, like most of its models, the compact SUV was expected to receive a mid-cycle refresh.
  • Hyundai is apparently going straight to the third-generation model instead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hyundai is skipping the typical mid-cycle refresh and plans to launch a completely redesigned Kona, with a sleek new style and an updated high-tech interior.

It’s been nearly four years since Hyundai introduced the second-generation Kona, meaning, like most of its models, the compact SUV was expected to receive a mid-cycle refresh.

Hyundai is apparently going straight to the third-generation model instead. Earlier this year, early-stage prototypes were spotted in Korea that looked much boxier and more rugged than the current Kona.

Since then, several test mules have been captured testing in the US, Europe, and other regions, confirming the Kona will adopt a more upright, traditional SUV design similar to the newly introduced Santa Fe, Palisade, and Tucson.

The wider, more powerful design appears to draw inspiration from Hyundai’s off-road Crater Concept, revealed at the LA Auto Show last year.

Hyundai remarked the off-road SUV Concept was a preview of the “next evolution” of its Extreme Rugged Terrain (XRT) vehicles, such as the IONIQ 5 XRT and Palisade XRT Pro. Is the Kona next in line to receive the XRT treatment?

A post shared by SHORTS CAR (@shorts_car).

Apparent leaked images from a few months ago revealed a design that looked like a mashup of the Crater Concept and IONIQ 5, with pixelated lighting and a clamshell hood.

In a recent development, most recently, the third-gen Hyundai Kona, codenamed “SX3,” was spotted disguised in a parking garage in Korea. The images were sent to ShortsCar, revealing the newly introduced Kona’s wheel design.

While earlier reports suggested Hyundai planned to drop the all-electric Kona variant and would only offer gas and hybrid versions, the prototype captured in Korea is expected to be the EV model. However, Hyundai has yet to confirm powertrain or battery specs.

In a recent development, the updates are even more evident on the inside. Previous spy images appeared to show the third-gen Hyundai Kona running Hyundai’s fresh Pleos Connect infotainment system, like the IONIQ 3.

In the IONIQ 3, Hyundai offers a 12.9″ or 14.6″ center infotainment screen, plus an optional driver display.

Like the current model, the third-gen Kona is expected to be available with fully electric (EV), hybrid, and gas-powered powertrains.

While Hyundai skipped the 2026 Kona EV, the electric version could return in 2027 or 2028 when the third-generation model is expected to arrive.

The hybrid version will likely use the same 1.6L hybrid engine as the new Seltos, while the EV variant could offer similar powertrain and battery options to the IONIQ 3.

The IONIQ 3 is available with two battery packs in Europe and the UK: 42 kWh and 61 kWh, offering WLTP ranges of up to 213 miles (344 km) and 308 miles (497 km), respectively.

Tesla stops selling every Cybertruck except the $109,990 Cyberbeast

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (803 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla is now only selling one version of the Cybertruck in the US: the tri-motor Cyberbeast, which just got another $7,500 price hike to $109,990.
  • The Dual Motor and Premium AWD trims are still listed on Tesla’s configurator, but both are greyed out and can’t be selected.
  • Here’s what Tesla’s US configurator reveals today with a Los Angeles delivery address:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla is now only selling one version of the Cybertruck in the US: the tri-motor Cyberbeast, which just got another $7,500 price hike to $109,990.

The Dual Motor and Premium AWD trims are still listed on Tesla’s configurator, but both are greyed out and can’t be selected. So the cheapest Cybertruck you can order today costs $109,990, up 57% from $69,990 in early August.

Here’s what Tesla’s US configurator reveals today with a Los Angeles delivery address:.

A week ago, the Cyberbeast cost $102,490. Before that, it was $99,990. That’s a $10,000 (10%) increase in about a week on a truck that hasn’t changed: 320 miles of estimated range, 11,000 lbs of towing, and 0-60 mph in 2.6 seconds.

It has been revealed that on November 6, the same day Elon Musk announced the end of Cybertruck production, Tesla raised Cybertruck prices by up to 10% and paused orders for the base Dual Motor. That made the $92,490 Premium AWD the entry point. Now it’s gone too, with no announcement. The configurator just stopped letting you pick it.

Newly introduced inventory isn’t an alternative either. When we checked, Tesla’s inventory search showed no new Cybertrucks within 200 miles of Los Angeles.

This comes two days after Musk extended Cybertruck production through the end of summer 2027 to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” On Monday, he claimed the order rate “far exceeds” production and that Tesla would “have to return deposits for a lot of people.”.

In a recent development, if there really is a backlog, cutting off the two cheaper trims is one way to cap it before the line shuts down. It also pushes whatever demand is left toward the most expensive, highest-margin version of the truck.

But the sales data doesn’t describe a truck with a demand problem in the other direction. We estimate Tesla delivered 7,000 to 8,000 Cybertrucks in Q3, a pace of about 30,000 a year on a line with more than 125,000 units of installed capacity. And in February, Tesla was offering a dual-motor Cybertruck at $59,990 for “only the next 10 days.”.

That’s $50,000 less than the cheapest Cybertruck you can order today. Nine months later.

Some of those $59,990 buyers are still waiting on delivery dates pushed into 2027. Tesla hasn’t said whether their orders, or any other Dual Motor and Premium orders in the queue, will be built before production ends.

Unlike the thousands of $59k CT orders that may never get manufactured I can guarantee that every high margin $110k CyberBeast order will be delivered before production ends.

Industry observers note that this is the wind-down playbook, and it’s moving faster than I expected. Announce the end, raise prices, pull the cheaper trims, and sell the last trucks in their most expensive form. Tesla is squeezing as much as it can out of every remaining Cybertruck.

I don’t blame Tesla for wanting margin on a program it’s walking away from. But it makes the “order backlog” talk look like what we said it was: an end-of-life rush Tesla created by announcing the end, now being monetized with a $109,990 sticker. Not great for anyone who was told in 2019 that this truck would start at $39,900, or that the tri-motor version would cost $69,900.

If you want a Cybertruck that isn’t a Cyberbeast, you’re now shopping used. And I’d keep an eye on used prices, because a truck that’s going out of production with no cheaper fresh option could hold its value better than it has over the last two years.

Industry observers note that A pair of workout leggings is the most key piece of activewear you’ll buy—but it’s also one of the hardest to get right. Too compressive and they dig in. Too soft and they stretch out after a few washes. And if they slide down mid-sprint or turn sheer in a squat, they’re done. Since Women’s Health was founded in 2005, our editors have sweat-tested workout leggings through strength training, long runs, Pilates, and HIIT to find pairs that stay opaque, supportive, and comfortable through every session.

To help you find the right leggings for every activity, I built the ultimate list, from great leggings for low-impact activities like yoga to the best compression leggings.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve trusted Nike leggings since my middle school days, circa 2012, and this pair is no exception. I love that the waistband never moves, no matter how much I bend, jump, run, or sweat. I’ve worn the original pair for years, but I love that the newest version has no front seam, for an even more flattering look. Pictured here is the flared version (which I love for lounging), but I typically reach for the standard legging silhouette for most workouts to avoid the extra fabric getting in the way.

Industry observers note that “I first tried these Nike leggings during the brand’s month-long running challenge in 2025, and they’ve stayed at the top of my extensive leggings drawer ever since,” indicates style contributor Lily Wohlner. “They allow me to move freely during all sorts of movements, they’re super durable, and are buttery soft for maximum comfort.”.

I find these leggings to be extremely flattering—even my mom told me I look good in them (that’s how you know they’re good!). The second you slip these on, every curve on your legs and thighs magically tightens thanks to the body-hugging nylon and spandex in the fabric. I also appreciate that Nike left out the side pockets with this pair, so they don’t add any width to the thighs. But, there’s still a back pocket that’s major enough to hold your phone, which is a welcome plus.

It has been revealed that these are one of my favorite leggings to run in because they stay in place. The high waistband never moves or slips down, so I never find myself adjusting it while in motion. At the gym, they’re stretchy enough to accommodate any move from deadlifts to downward dog, but they still have enough compression to make me feel held in and supported. I’ve done my fair share of squats in these leggings—I actually wore them during a few lower-body training sessions—and they pass the squat test every time. Another bonus? They’re super moisture-wicking, so I worry less about sweat stains peeking through at the gym.

If you're not the biggest fan of high-rise leggings, don't worry—they also come in a mid-rise fit. Plus, they have raw cut edges, so they can easily be tucked into your fave socks without any bunching in sight. They are super flattering, and they've garnered the most compliments I've ever received from a pair of leggings.

At $105 they are on the pricer side, but they’ve never once declined in quality since I’ve owned them, and I’ve probably washed them over 80 times.

Sources indicate that I’ve been singing praises for Crz Yoga ever since I joined the team at Women’s Health over a year ago. The affordable brand makes some of the best workout clothes on Amazon with quality that actually competes with high-end labels. Think: smooth, stretchy fabric that holds up over tons of wear and wash cycles.

Recent findings suggest that the 81% nylon and 19% elastane blend (aka the brand’s famed Butterluxe fabric) has the second-skin softness and light-to-moderate compression that feels good during just about any workout. I love the high-rise waistband that doesn’t slip down during HIIT workouts, weight lifting, or long walks.

This pair even earned a spot in our guide to the best leggings with pockets for the dual side pockets that securely hold small essentials like a keycard or headphones without adding too much bulk to the hips. Oh, and I love that it comes in a ton of colors (most of them with sports bras to match!), from classic neutrals to brighter, bolder shades.

My only con is that it only comes in a single length, which may bunch slightly at the ankles on petite frames, and while the pockets are handy, they’re not the most secure option for larger phones during high-impact workouts.

Industry observers note that for a long time, I always opted for the softest, stretchiest leggings in my drawer, no matter the workout. However, in the past year, I’ve been doing a lot more strength training, and I’ve found myself swapping soft pairs for more compressive options like the Wunder Train to stay locked in and supported during moves like jump squats, burpees, and quick-burst movements. I never thought I’d be a compression leggings gal, but once I tried them, I never went back.

According to recent reports, the Wunder Train Leggings are made out of 77 percent nylon and 23 percent elastane (a light, stretchy fabric). The higher elastane content makes them super stretchy. During my weekly Barry's HIIT workout class, these leggings stay put and keep me feeling secure, supported, and snatched. With softer leggings, I’m always adjusting them or feeling like they don’t offer enough support during deep bends and hinges. The hidden drawstring in the waistband of these leggings also helps.One of my top priorities when it comes to leggings is absolutely no sweat stains. And this pair nails it thanks to the sweat-wicking nylon, which is super durable and keeps you dry. I’ve had some seriously sweaty gym sessions in them, and while sweat does build up after intense workouts, it dries way faster than other leggings I’ve tried thanks to its high nylon content in the fabric. I also love how the fabric feels light, breathable, and cool against the skin, so it doesn’t cause overheating like some of my other leggings. That said, I only own these in darker colors, so I can’t speak to how well they hide sweat stains on lighter shades.

I’ve tried a ton of pieces from Rhone, like its workout dress and bra tops, but my favorites are these pocket leggings, which have tons of storage for my belongings, just enough compression, and maximum softness.

Unlike many other pocketed leggings I’ve tried, these offer a sleek look—you can barely even notice the pockets. While discreet, the pockets still hold a ton. I can even fit my iPhone in them, and thanks to the pockets’ compression, it won’t slip out. Unlike most leggings with pockets, these don’t add any bulk to the thighs for a flattering finish.

I’ve worn these leggings during many different types of workouts, and they always strike the perfect balance of support and comfort. These are soft enough for a stretching or yoga class, but really shine in any exercise that gets your heart rate pumping and the sweat flowing. Plus, the moisture-wicking fabric and its odor-fighting finish keep me feeling fresh, even when things get super sweaty.

In a recent development, I’m also a mega fan of the wide waistband that stays put through any exercise. And get this: If you’re out in the sun, these leggings add a great extra layer of defense to your sunscreen, as they’re equipped with UPF 50 for sun protection.

My one con with these leggings is that they run large, as does all of Rhone’s womenswear. I would size down if you’re looking for a normal fit with light compression.

According to recent reports, beyond Yoga leggings in their signature (super soft) Spacedye fabric have been my go-to for lounging and low-impact yoga for years. But recently, the activewear label dropped Glowzone, its new high-performance line with a snappy fabric designed to support intense, sweaty movement while still offering the comfort we know and love.

The Glowzone fabric is made of smooth nylon and a bit more elastane than the brand’s famed Spacedye fabric, giving it noticeably more compression. It’s snappy and compressive enough that it keeps me feeling supported and locked-in during my workouts without restricting movement or sliding down my waist (something I often have trouble with while wearing other compressive leggings).

Despite the more snappy fabric, it’s every bit as soft and comfortable as I’d expect from a pair of Beyond Yoga leggings. I still reach for mine on more chill days spent walking the boardwalk near the beach or running errands around town—but the material is just a touch too compressive to wear for lazy days spent couch rotting. Where it really shines is for working out: I’ve worn it to the gym for cardio and lifting sessions as well as mat Pilates classes, and I love that I can basically forget about what I’m wearing while I focus on getting my reps in.

In a recent development, contributor Sidney Lee tested a few items from the Glowzone collection and agrees the fabric is every bit as soft as she hoped. “It’s slightly thinner than Spacedye, which makes Glowzone feel sleeker and more breathable against the skin,” she notes. “Also, the four-way stretch and moisture-wicking technology of the new fabric offer more freedom of movement, especially during heated classes or summer workouts.”.

Sources indicate that another huge bonus? This pair is basically seamless (the only seams are located on the inside of the legs and at the buttock) so there’s no rubbing or chafing. There’s no front seam (which helps keep the fit looking flattering, if you know what I mean), and it has raw edges at the bottom, which means the legging basically melts into your skin.

Gymshark's bestselling leggings are incredibly breathable and dry swiftly. Nylon is a synthetic fabric that’s hydrophobic (i.e it resists the penetration of water), so these leggings are great for wicking sweat away from the body. Not only that, but they’re made with breathable mesh dots to help keep you cool during tough workouts. Of all the leggings I’ve tested, this pair does the best job of keeping me sweat-free even after the most intense sweat sessions. Even after a particularly grueling Barry’s class, I was dry by the time I walked out the door.

This legging is nearly seamless—the only seams are on the back buttock area— which helps shape the glutes—and on the inside of each leg. Lauture adds that this pair of leggings also does a great job at holding you in. “It might take you a few moments of jumping up and down to get them on, but they feel great on your body once you get them up,” she indicates. These leggings lean on the compressive side, but tighter leggings are great for higher intensity workouts because they hold you in. So, if you’re into HIIT, running, or strength training, this is another solid pair. Since they’re slightly tighter, I find that they shape and sculpt your body in all the right places.

There are no pockets at the legs or in the waistband of these leggings, so if you don’t need storage, these are a great option.

Of all the leggings I've tested, Spanx has the best smoothing fabric. They’re not super compressive (which is why I love them for low-impact exercises), but the fabric is insanely soft, sweat-wicking, and buttery smooth.

Alo's High-Waist Airbrush Leggings are super versatile because they’re nice and compressive for the gym, and their sleek look plays well with all my casual fits for a chic brunch look.

An Anthropic mathematician indicates Claude helped him crack the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old puzzle with a $1 million prize attached.

His claim surfaced Friday, one day after the AI company’s stock-market debut, and has not yet been independently verified.

It has been revealed that “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Levent Alpöge wrote in a four-page note. He notes the method also resolves the broader Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, which extends the question to other mathematical functions.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

It has been revealed that alpöge claims he and Claude encoded their argument in Lean, software used to check mathematical proofs step by step. His note links to 14 downloadable parts of the proof archive, but its availability does not amount to acceptance by the mathematical community.

It has been revealed that alpöge says he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about a possible announcement “late Sunday night,” November 15. He then consulted company leadership and noted there was a constraint to respect, without explaining precisely what it was.

“The precise timing is horrible,” he acknowledged. Alpöge rejected a cynical interpretation of the timing, but did not explicitly say the company’s IPO caused the delay.

Anthropic began trading on Nasdaq Thursday, November 19, after raising $81.34 billion in its offering.

According to recent reports, alpöge figured in September’s AI math wars. OpenAI claimed it had solved the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem as he and NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster pursued related fluid-equation work, sparking a credit dispute over research priority.

Sources indicate that openAI followed in October with 722 manuscripts generated by an unreleased model, grouped into 372 families of results. Only 162 included Lean-checked main results, and mathematicians demanded stronger evidence rather than accepting the company’s flood of claims at face value.

It has been revealed that some mathematicians fear a “mathocalypse,” with AI solving coveted problems before researchers can learn from pursuing them. Toronto mathematician Daniel Litt warned that, without adaptation, “there’s just no more math in 50 years.” At an MIT panel this week, Buckmaster argued mathematics still requires human understanding.

First posed by Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis predicts where certain zeros of the Riemann zeta function fall. The question matters because those zeros are linked to the distribution of prime numbers, whose patterns underlie extensive mathematical research.

A proof would be a historic mathematical result, since experts have been trying to solve that for over a century.

Lean can verify that formal deductions obey its rules. Mathematicians still need to reproduce the archive, check the formalized theorem matches the original conjecture, and examine the claimed result before considering it settled.

Anthropic previously reported progress on the zeta function without claiming to solve the full hypothesis. Alpöge’s latest assertion goes far beyond that earlier work.

The Clay Mathematics Institute lists the Riemann hypothesis among its Millennium Prize Problems, each carrying a $1 million award. Under the institute’s prize rules, a proposed solution must be published in a qualifying outlet, survive at least two years of scrutiny, and earn general acceptance before the prize can be considered.

Volkswagen is delaying another EV based on the SSP

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (636 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After delaying development of the long-awaited electric Golf, Volkswagen is delaying another EV based on its SSP platform.
  • As it scrambles to cut costs, Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer revealed in an internal memo at the end of October that development of the all-electric Golf is being delayed at its Wolfsburg plant in Germany.
  • The news comes after the VW Group posted an operating loss of €5.9 billion ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter, its largest quarterly loss since the infamous Dieselgate scandal in 2015.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After delaying development of the long-awaited electric Golf, Volkswagen is delaying another EV based on its SSP platform.

As it scrambles to cut costs, Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer revealed in an internal memo at the end of October that development of the all-electric Golf is being delayed at its Wolfsburg plant in Germany.

The news comes after the VW Group posted an operating loss of €5.9 billion ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter, its largest quarterly loss since the infamous Dieselgate scandal in 2015.

“We simply can’t afford this work right now,” Schäfer remarked in the memo reviewed by Reuters. The Wolfsburg plant, AKA the “heart of the VW brand,” is about €300 million ($334.5 million) short of its cost-cutting targets, the memo said.

Volkswagen initially planned to launch the Golf EV in 2028, but Schäfer unveiled earlier this year that the long-awaited electric car was delayed until closer to 2030.

Schäfer suggested the delay was because the SSP (Scalable Systems Platform), which is being developed through its partnership with Rivian, was taking longer than expected, again due to costs.

According to Autocar, Volkswagen is now delaying the Audi A4 E-tron as well, another vehicle that was initially planned to be among the first based on the SSP platform.

Production of the electric A4 is being pushed back until at least 2029, a year later than originally planned. While the delay is disappointing for Audi fans (including myself) still waiting for an electric A4, it also puts Audi behind rival luxury brands in the mid-size sedan segment.

BMW has the latest i3, and Mercedes-Benz has the C-Class EV, both of which feature major improvements in range, charging, and efficiency over their previous-generation EVs.

Volkswagen noted in 2023 that the 800V SSP will serve as a “single future backbone with integrated electric and electronics architecture,” claiming that more than 40 million models were expected to be built on it.

The organization also stated investment and R&D costs were expected to be reduced by about 30% compared to the current MEB platform, enabling most models “to achieve the same margin compared to their conventionally powered counterparts.”.

Volkswagen’s software struggles started in its internal division, Cariad, leading to delays, missed targets, and budget overruns.

To fix it, VW turned to Rivian, forming a joint venture to develop its next-gen software-defined vehicle (SDV) electrical architecture.

In March, VW mentioned several test vehicles, including the ID.EVERY1, Audi, and Scout with the SDV architecture underwent “comprehensive evaluation,” and successfully validated over-the-air (OTA) functionality.

Being cash efficient is good, but delays to the next-gen platform that will keep you competitive with rival brands seem like a problem.

Industry observers note that however, the Audi A4 E-tron delay is not entirely about software. The Autocar report claims Audi demanded significant changes to the SSP platform for the A4 E-tron so it more closely matched the current gas version.

Audi reportedly wanted individual footwells for front and rear passengers, which would require repositioning the battery.

The luxury brand also reportedly asked for a 48V electrical system instead of the traditional 12V setup initially planned.

In a recent development, while development of the Golf EV is on hold, VW’s works council noted the pause will not delay its launch, promising to make up for lost time. It’s still expected to launch in 2030. The Audi A4 E-tron is now expected to arrive around 2029.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that few artisanal traditions are so linked with a place that its geographical namesake winds up in the global lexicon. In the case of fine wool shawls from Kashmir—prized among 19th-century Europeans, including Joséphine Bonaparte—the word cashmere stuck. For Kadri Mujtaba, a fascination with these textiles came early. Born into a family of merchants and weavers in the region’s city of Srinagar, he observed a deep-rooted culture around hand-spun yarn and small wooden looms.

A bouquet of lotus pods held up against the brand’s Mountain blanket in pine.

One of the studio’s handmade shawl looms.

A Doorway Sozni twill blanket draped over a chair.

In a recent development, “It’s the original work-from-home idea,” he says of the technique, passed down for centuries. Amid encroaching mechanization, Mujtaba has stayed committed to slow craft, cultivating a network of some 2,000 artisans over the past two decades. Initially he’d create custom pieces for designers and brands (Pierre Yovanovitch, The Row, Luis Laplace) and host high-end trunk demonstrates. That is how Jonathan Renker—via his father, a longtime customer—first encountered the wares. Now, he and Mujtaba have partnered on Kadri: a new brand of cashmere accessories and home goods that marry Kashmiri refinement and streamlined design.

A Jaali Kaani blanket on the grounds of Pari Mahal garden.

A wood swift of cashmere yarn at the Kadri atelier.

Shawls and scarves from Kadri’s debut collection.

The tech giant debuts with a collection of scarves, throws, and blankets. The cofounders enlisted creative director Dan Thawley and textile designer Maeva Elfassi, who distilled the Kashmir Valley landscape into shades of tobacco, lime, vermilion, and—as a nod to Srinagar’s Dal Lake—dusty blue. Wool from Changthangi goats, which graze across the plateaus of nearby Ladakh, is spun by hand, resulting in airy, ultrasoft knits. More impressive still is the subtlety on display. A bouclé piece has the immersive pull of a Color Field painting, while a quilted scarf joins two paper-thin layers. Just one blanket requires months of work and a balletic dance of bobbins.

According to recent reports, “What makes Kadri so special is this research-and-development approach,” notes Renker, describing a push toward novel applications while holding fast to the handmade vernacular. “The only electricity that’s used are the overhead lights on a cloudy day.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health update on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.
  • The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.
  • Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health update on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.

Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.

In two podcast episodes released October 20, Applegate revealed that doctors had told her she was misdiagnosed with MS.

Sources indicate that “She came into my room and said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS,’ ” Applegate said as she fought back tears. “I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.”.

The “Anchorman” and “Dead to Me” actor explained that her symptoms have continued to worsen, leaving her without an explanation for what she’s experiencing as doctors investigate the cause.

Being misdiagnosed with MS is relatively common. Applegate’s revelation highlights a difficult reality for people living with unexplained symptoms resembling MS. Her experience raises questions about how MS is diagnosed, why misdiagnoses may occur, and what people can do when their symptoms don’t match their diagnosis.

While MS can be difficult to diagnose, an accurate diagnosis can help people with the condition gain access to appropriate treatment. A misdiagnosis, on the other hand, may lead to unnecessary interventions and medication, and take an emotional toll over time.

“MS can be challenging to diagnose because there is no single test that confirms it in every case,” stated Steve Allder, MD, consultant neurologist at Re:Cognition Health.

“An incorrect diagnosis can have significant consequences. Someone incorrectly diagnosed with MS may experience considerable anxiety, undergo unnecessary investigations, or receive treatments with potential risks and side effects. Equally, if MS is missed, treatment may be delayed, potentially allowing further neurological damage,” Allder told Healthline.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis underscores that MS misdiagnoses remain a concern.

Research suggests that around 15% of people diagnosed with MS may actually have another condition.

However, estimates vary across studies, with some reporting rates ranging from 5–41%.

While an accurate diagnosis can guide patients toward appropriate treatment, a mistaken one may lead to unnecessary medication, emotional distress, and years of uncertainty.

Fresh diagnostic guidelines offer hope for greater accuracy, but they also raise important questions about how doctors can adequately distinguish MS from other conditions.

“Research has shown that MS can be both overdiagnosed and underdiagnosed,” Allder noted.

In a recent development, “Diagnosis relies on a combination of symptoms, neurological examination, MRI findings, and sometimes, additional tests. It is also crucial to recognize that diagnoses can evolve as new evidence emerges. As neurologists, we must remain open to revisiting a diagnosis when symptoms or test results do not fit, ensuring patients receive appropriate treatment and support.”.

In a recent development, MS symptoms may vary widely and overlap with several other conditions. These may include:.

Because these conditions share certain features with MS, healthcare professionals should consider a patient’s full clinical profile rather than relying on a single symptom or scan.

In a recent development, “MS can cause numbness, tingling, muscle weakness, visual disturbances, balance problems, and fatigue. However, these symptoms are not unique to the condition,” Allder said.

It has been revealed that “For example, numbness and tingling may indicate peripheral neuropathy, sometimes associated with diabetes or vitamin B12 deficiency. Weakness or altered sensation may result from a trapped nerve or spinal cord compression. Migraines can cause visual disturbances and sensory symptoms, while inner-ear disorders may affect balance,” he continued.

Allder noted that fatigue is particularly nonspecific and may be associated with:.

He explained that, as a neurologist, he considers the pattern, duration, and progression of symptoms alongside examination findings.

“No single symptom automatically indicates MS. A thorough assessment is essential to identify the underlying cause and ensure the patient receives appropriate treatment,” he said.

There is no single test that definitively confirms every case of MS.

Diagnosis typically involves reviewing symptoms, conducting neurological examinations, and evaluating MRI scans and laboratory results.

MRI findings may be tricky to interpret. Some white-matter spots resemble MS lesions but may result from migraine, aging, or other conditions. Misapplying diagnostic criteria or overlooking alternative explanations can also lead to mistakes.

“MRI abnormalities alone do not confirm MS,” Allder said. “The diagnosis must be based on the overall clinical picture, with alternative explanations carefully considered.”.

Research also suggests that MS misdiagnosis rates may differ by sex.

Research shows females are 2.1 times more likely to be misdiagnosed with MS than males, highlighting the potential for diagnostic bias and differences in how symptoms are evaluated.

The updated MS diagnostic criteria published in 2025 offer a framework for improving diagnosis.

The updated guidelines introduce several notable changes.

For instance, the optic nerve (the nerve connecting the eye to the brain) is now included as a fifth anatomical location for assessing evidence of MS.

The revised criteria also include new MRI biomarkers, such as the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions. These features can help doctors distinguish MS-related abnormalities from other conditions.

These changes may help doctors diagnose MS earlier and more accurately.

In a recent development, if you experience persistent or recurring neurological symptoms, seek medical advice. Your doctor can assess your symptoms and, if applicable, refer you to a neurologist.

Sudden weakness, vision loss, or difficulty speaking requires urgent medical assessment, Allder remarked.

“Depending on the findings, investigations may include MRI scans of the brain and spinal cord, blood tests, and, in some cases, a lumbar puncture,” Allder noted.

“It is important that results are interpreted alongside symptoms and examination findings, as no single test should determine the diagnosis in isolation.”.

Allder remarked that if you’re unsure about a diagnosis, you can ask your neurologist what evidence supports it and whether alternative health conditions have been considered.

Industry observers note that “A second opinion or follow-up assessment may be appropriate. The priority is an accurate diagnosis that leads to the right treatment and support,” Allder noted.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A GREAT PAIR of sunglasses is the easiest way to upgrade your look. The right style can sharpen angular faces, soften sharper ones, or dress up even the most basic outfit—think square frames adding structure to a round face, or classic aviators elevating a T-shirt and jeans. They also protect your eyes from UV rays and cut down on glare, so you’re covered in both style and function. When picking your next pair, think about face shape and classic silhouettes.

Sources indicate that since 2020, our Men’s Health fashion team has tested over 50 styles—including aviators, wayfarers, and rounded frames—which all have stood the test of time due to their durability, versatility, and style. And don’t forget about occasions—what you wear to the beach, on a hike, or just around the city should match both your lifestyle and how you want to show up.

It has been revealed that as a style editor for the past four years, I’ve tested over 25 different pairs of sunnies, but the Ray-Ban Wayfarer is still the best in its class. The signature silhouette—a slightly angular trapezoidal shape with thicker acetate frames—adds structure without looking too sharp, so it looks great on just about all round, oval, and even square faces and plays well with just about every fit.

Industry observers note that first introduced in the ’50s as a casual alternative to metal frames, it was later worn by Tom Cruise, Michael Jackson, and George Michael, cementing its style icon status by the ’80s. In the past few years, Ray-Ban has updated it with a few stylish design tweaks—including a slightly smaller frame and more rounded lens shapes. We found it’s even easier to wear day-to-day to the office, lunch, or an early happy hour.

A wide range of frame and lens colors are available in the Original Wayfarer, but you can’t ever go wrong with the old-school black. We love this style because it looks great with every kind of vibe: a tailored suit, a tee and jeans, or just swim trunks on vacation. I found the acetate frame to be extra robust and heavy-duty at withstanding impact, courtesy of the seven-barrel hinges on each side. While this design does make the whole thing a bit heavier than most sunnies on this list, I never feel like it’s a burden on my face. I’ve found them comfortable whether I’m wearing them for a couple hours or from sunup to sundown.

Read More: Best Sunglasses Brands for Men.

The Downing from Warby Parker is a safe bet because it will never go out of style. The slightly rounded shape traces back to midcentury optical styles that leaned more circular before chunkier shapes took over the game. That softer, more classic silhouette flatters square to angular face shapes especially well, and gives the Downing its staying power today. While heritage brands like Ray-Ban and Persol offer similar rounded styles, Warby Parker delivers a comparable timeless look and build at a much more accessible price.

The rounded lenses help soften sharper, more angular faces, but they’re not overly circular, which is why they still work on round and oval faces too. It’s one of those rare shapes that’s versatile across the board. I have a round face, and they look great with whatever vibe I’m going with. The keyhole bridge sits naturally on the nose (no adjustable pads), though it may not be a perfect fit for guys with lower or higher nose bridges. The acetate frame feels smooth yet durable, and the scratch-resistant lenses hold well if you drop them or toss them in your bag.

I also found that the temples are lightweight, so they don’t pinch behind your ears, making them easy to wear from the time I get to the office to the time I leave. The color—called English Oak—is like a toned-down tortoise that looks best with solid, everyday staples.

If you want a pair of sunglasses that you can throw on with anything, every day, The Napoli is the one. I’ve worn them with everything—think T-shirt and jeans, a polo and chinos, or even a hoodie and shorts. The square shape adds structure to rounder faces without looking too boxy on guys with sharper features. The keyhole bridge sits so comfortably on the nose, I don’t even feel it. I love the lens colors, which veer away from the super dark black lenses.

The gradient brown-to-yellow lenses are easy on the eyes in bright sun, giving a relaxed vibe. This also makes the sunnies more wearable—you can rock them in the bright sun or just walk around the city without feeling like you’re hiding behind your shades. The temples are slim but stay in place no matter how I move my head. While the acetate frame is lightweight and comfortable, it doesn’t offer the same durability as heavier acetate, so handle with care if you’re rough on glasses or tend to toss them in your bag.

Randolph began churning out military-spec aviators for the U.S. Air Force in the late 1970s, and its metal frames are still very stylish today. Unlike mass-produced sunglasses, each pair is handcrafted in the U.S., going through 200 steps over six weeks, which gives them a high-quality feel built to last a lifetime. I’ve had mine for three years now and wore them for the first time during a weekend getaway to Nantucket. I sported them on boat rides, walking along the pier, and during casual dinners. They performed flawlessly, reducing glare on the water and staying comfortable for hours. They’re perfect for everyday casual outfits like shorts, T-shirts, or polo shirts. They also pair nicely with slightly dressier looks, like linen button-downs or lightweight jackets.

The Skytech glass lenses are made from durable optical glass and deliver exceptional clarity, contrast, and anti-reflective performance, with both polarized and nonpolarized options available. The durable matte chrome frames with snug screws hold up well, while the clear bayonet-style temple tips slide gently along the side of your head instead of curving around your ears. They make the sunglasses easy to slip on and off and help them stay in place. This aviator shape works for most face types but is especially flattering on oval, square, and heart-shaped faces, balancing wider foreheads and softening softer jawlines. It’s not the best option for wider faces as it can make them appear even bigger.

Oakley’s Radar EV Path has those taller lenses perfect for athletes and anyone who spends a lot of time running, golfing, or cycling. This extended range of view really indicates off the legendary Prizm lens, which makes colors pop and boosts contrast so you can see everything clearly. This wraparound design gives you extra coverage at the top, protecting your eyes from sunlight, wind, and debris. The no-slip nosepad and extended arms keep the glasses locked in place, even when you're sweating.

The lightweight, flexible frame plus adjustable nosepiece makes them comfortable for long sessions. Best for oval and medium-to-long faces, the wraparound style hugs the sides for a snug, secure fit. Small or very round faces can still wear them, but wider faces might find them a little tight. Heads-up: These are just made for performance and not style, so don’t try to sport them with a casual T-shirt or button-up at a dressy brunch.

Recent findings suggest that uniqlo delivers an affordable rectangular pair of sunglasses that don’t feel cheap. They look as sharp and polished as pairs that cost way more. The frames are made from flexible plastic that feel lightweight in hand but aren’t flimsy. Case in point: I dropped them more than once and even accidentally sat on them—fully expecting a snap. Somehow, the temples held strong and didn’t split in half. The thicker temples help here, too. The bridge and nose pads are molded into the frame, providing comfortable support. This pair of sunglasses lacks adjustable nose pads, so the fit may not work for those who have a low or high nose bridge.

According to recent reports, the rectangular shape is especially great for rounder or softer face shapes, adding structure and making your features look sharper. If you’ve got a fuller face, this is one of the easiest ways to balance things out. Yes, these shades block sunlight effectively with enough coverage to keep glare out of your eyes without feeling oversized. I wore them on bright midday walks and didn’t find myself having to squint. If you’re looking for multiple color frames, Uniqlo doesn’t offer that with these shades. You can only get them in black, but that doesn’t limit your styling options.

Sources indicate that ray-Ban’s round sunglasses are a step up from your everyday pair, thanks to the gold metal rims and classic green lenses, which give off a more luxe, retro aesthetic. The thin metal build looks great and keeps the pair lightweight and sleek, but it’s more delicate than thicker frames.

Sources indicate that the metal bridge with adjustable nose pads lets you fine-tune the fit, while the slim temples keep them comfortable. It’s perfect for vacation fits—easily pairing with swim trunks or an open camp shirt and linen shorts for a resort lunch. I’ve worn mine poolside in Costa Rica while lying in the sun, but they’ll also dress something like a tee and jeans if you don’t want to look too basic. It sits a bit closer to the face (petite fit), which makes it feel more styled than oversized. The round shape softens sharper features, but still works across the board for most guys. Bonus: These Ray-Ban’s come in a bunch of lens options—blue, brown, and gradients—so you can switch up the vibe.

Sources indicate that tortoise sunglasses are timeless, versatile, and universally flattering. This classy pair from Moscot looks good with lots of neutral items—think white tees, navy shirts, or olive chinos. You can also mix it with small or muted patterns like thin stripes, tiny checks, or small prints. These shades are made from real Italian acetate and come in a square-ish round silhouette that’ll always be in style. It’s offered in four sizes for a tailored fit. The keyhole nose bridge keeps them comfortable for more than six hours, and the rims feel robust without feeling overly heavy.

The rounded lenses work best on round and oval faces, thanks to its slight square edge that balances softer features. Caveat: Guys with very square or angular faces may find that the softer edges of this frame don’t add much definition, so the effect is more relaxed than structured. Also, I found these sunnies to be heavier than other picks that I’ve tested, which may feel bulky on smaller faces. They come in over 20 color options, but for an everyday classic look, the chestnut fade is a safe bet.

Sources indicate that persol's aviator shades offer a wider field of view and a serious level of coverage. These bold, square sunglasses are a great option for guys with round faces, but anyone can sport them.

Industry observers note that in our testing, we found that the polarized, light blue lenses not only looked dope, but also offered scratch and shatter resistance to make sure these sunnies last a while. They look great worn for a lunch date with friends, but give real main character energy when you're tanning on the beach or poolside.

Recent findings suggest that another stylish but also functional standout is the 100 percent acetate frame, which we've found to be lightweight and sturdy. After using it for a full day at the beach, we hardly noticed that we were actually wearing it.

Rectangular sunglasses tend to look best on guys with rounded, oval, or heart-shaped faces. If that’s you, say hello to Oliver Peoples' version, which is a collaboration with tennis champ Roger Federer. Their sharper edges complement guys with softer facial features.

We found that these sunnies offer high-optical quality as well as style for days spent on and off the tennis court. Thanks to the adjustable rubber nose pads and temple tips, they rested gently on our face (even when we were playing) and felt more comfortable to wear all day long than any other rectangular frames we tested.

In a recent development, look for frames that add structure—think square, rectangular, or angular aviators and wayfarers. These shapes balance softer features and make your face appear more defined.

Most frame shapes work, from round to square. Experiment with classic aviators, bold wayfarers, or even a round lens for a vintage vibe.

Opt for rounded or oval frames that soften a strong jawline. Circle lenses or softer rectangle shapes can help create balance.

Frames that are wider at the bottom or slightly curved help balance a broader forehead. Aviators, teardrop lenses, or rounded frames are good options.

High cheekbones and a narrow forehead and chin look great with rimless or oval frames of sunglasses because they emphasize your eyes and soften your facial angles.

When choosing a upcoming pair of sunglasses, you should make sure that they provide 100 percent UV protection against both UVA and UVB rays. Otherwise, you can find yourself in a world of problems. "Excessive sun exposure could lead to cataracts and eye or eyelid cancer," Jeff Pettey, MD, clinical spokesperson for the American Academy of Ophthalmology, previously told MH. You don't have to spend a fortune on sunglasses, but it's a must that you find a pair that fits well. As for what type to consider, go with wraparound models as they block UV rays that come in from the side and shield against winds that can cause dry eyes.

Recent findings suggest that polarized lenses are designed to cut down harsh glare, which helps reduce eye strain and makes it easier to see clearly in bright conditions. That glare usually comes from light bouncing off flat surfaces like water, snow, or pavement, not just direct sunlight. Polarized technology works by filtering out light, so you’re not squinting or dealing with that blinding shine. Because of that, polarized sunglasses are especially useful for water sports and outdoor activities, while photochromic lenses (which adjust to changing light) are recommended for everyday use.

Finding the right pair of sunglasses has everything to do with a frame that works for your face, style, and how you live in them. Certain shapes can sharpen your features or balance them out, while the right style can pull together everything from a laid-back weekend fit to a more polished look. That’s why we focused on aviators, wayfarers, round, square, and sport frames—the same ones our team has tested across everyday wear, travel, and outdoor activities—so you’re getting options that look good and hold up in real situations.

To find the best sunglasses for men, our Men’s Health fashion team—led by Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan—has tested over 50 pairs since 2021. That means everything from daily commutes and office fits to tropical getaways, beach days, and long weekends on the water, along with more active use like running, hiking, and biking. We put each pair through the same hands-on process, evaluating style, comfort, fit, durability, and overall value.

Sources indicate that we paid close attention to how they held up over time—whether the frames could handle sweat and movement, if the lenses reduced glare and eye strain, and whether they delivered reliable 100 percent UV protection. Just as important, we looked at versatility: Could one pair work across multiple settings, from casual everyday wear to more dressed-up occasions? We also compared them against top competitors in the category to make sure each pick truly stands out in its class. Read on for the best sunglasses for men from classic brands like Ray-Ban and Randolph to newcomers like Jimmy Fairly Paris to sporty ones like Oakley.

It has been revealed that acetate is a popular material for crafting frames since it combines both durability and style, allowing for a wide range of color and pattern options, and is thus frequently used in premium sunglasses. TR-90, a thermoplastic material, is known for its durability, flexibility, and resistance to impact, and thus can often be found in outdoorsy sunglasses. Nylon is lightweight and flexible while offering excellent durability, even being able to resist extreme temperatures. Other materials like stainless steel and titanium are simply no-brainers due to their outstanding durability and ability to withstand wear and tear over time.

BYD’s upcoming flagship Tang SUV starts at about $34,000 with two enormous screens

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that BYD opened pre-orders for the third-generation Tang starting at about $34,000 in China.
  • The third-generation Tang joins the Great Tang, or Da Tang, as it’s called in China in BYD’s expanding flagship SUV lineup.
  • We knew it was coming soon after the new model appeared in a regulatory filing in China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) last month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that BYD opened pre-orders for the third-generation Tang starting at about $34,000 in China. This five-seat flagship SUV packs more than you’d expect for the money, with two massive 30-inch-plus screens inside and up to 850 km (528 miles) of CLTC range.

The third-generation Tang joins the Great Tang, or Da Tang, as it’s called in China in BYD’s expanding flagship SUV lineup.

We knew it was coming soon after the new model appeared in a regulatory filing in China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) last month.

BYD revealed on Friday that pre-orders for the third-gen Tang are officially open, starting at 225,000 yuan, which is around $34,000.

The “large five-seat flagship SUV,” as BYD calls it, is available in three variants, priced from 225,000 yuan ($34,000), 240,000 yuan ($36,000), and 260,000 yuan ($39,000) with rear- and all-wheel-drive variants.

The two lower-priced variants are both RWD, offering a CLTC range of up to 850 km (528 miles), while the top-spec dual-motor AWD version has up to 770 km (478 miles).

All versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging tech, enabling the battery to be charged from 10% to 80% in five minutes, or nine minutes to go from 10% to 97%.

Recent findings suggest that inside, the five-seat SUV packs a surprising amount of tech and premium extras for the price. The setup features two massive screens: a 35.4″ integrated display and another 30″ panoramic theater screen.

Unlike its predessor, which offered five and six-seat configurations, the third-gen Tang will only be offered as a five-seater.

The five-seat setup opens up interior space for passengers and the third-gen Tang has the largest front trunk (frunk) in its class at 205L, BYD said.

Like many of its latest flagship vehicles, the third-gen Tang is equipped with BYD’s latest tech, including its God’s Eye B driver-assistance system and Disus-A dual-chamber intelligent air suspension body control system.

Other added features include a 22-speaker Dynaudio sound system, intelligent electric all‑wheel drive, a high-speed tire blowout stability system, and its iTAC intelligent torque control system.

Lu Tian, the general manager of BYD’s Dynasty division mentioned third-gen Tang vehicles have arrived at dealerships nationwide.

Why mention "two enormous screens" like they are some markers of a more premium vehicle or represent some value? We don't measure the utility of cars by screen real estate per dollar. It's the other part of the utility that matter: range, driving dynamics, road trip convenience, fit/finish/materials/insulation. Personally, I don't think "enormous screens" are going to age well as an automotive trend.

The Great Tang received over 150,000 preorders by the time it launched in mid-June, a record for a single BYD model.

Since its official launch, the larger Great Tang (Da Tang) has sold more than 10,000 units for four straight months now.

According to recent reports, the Great Tang is on sale in China in pure electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains. The cheapest EV variant starts at 239,900 yuan ($35,500) a CLTC driving range of 800 km (497 miles). Starting at just 269,900 yuan ($40,000), the Flagship EV version uses a bigger (130.15 kWh) battery, offering a CLTC range of up to 590 miles (950 km).

Will BYD’s smaller five-seat SUV draw the same demand? Let us know your thoughts in the comments below.

#110024. Experts Warn That a Deadly Disease That Causes ‘Immune Amnesia’ Is Surging in the U.S.
