📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The German shepherd was originally bred to do exactly what their name implies, but a lot has changed since Max von Stephanitz introduced the breed in 1899. Today, the German shepherd is one of the world’s most recognizable and popular dogs, largely due to their intelligence, trainability, and companionship. You’re just as likely to spot one of them at an airport sniffing for contraband as you are at a kennel club competition.

But a good “work” German shepherd and a good show dog require two very different sets of traits. According to researchers at Sweden’s Uppsala University, these specific qualities are so pronounced that they’re even visible at the genetic level. What’s more, many of these genes can also be seen in humans.

“It’s interesting that we can now see that this selective breeding has indeed led to differences between working dogs and show dogs among German shepherds—differences that can be seen at both the behavioral and genetic levels,” Uppsala University genomics researcher Kerstin Lindblad-Toh explained in a recent profile.

Lindblad-Toh and her colleagues laid out their findings in a study recently published in the journal Animal Genetics. To assess the iconic breed, the team reviewed a massive dataset of 23,000 German shepherds who previously participated in a standardized behavioral test known as the Dog Mentality Assessment (DMA). During the DMA, canines are exposed to a range of situations, such as meeting strangers, play time, and even encountering imposing, ghostly figures. The team discovered that while German shepherds often scored higher for traits like neuroticism and shyness, the breed’s working dogs generally exhibited more curiosity, less fear, and a willingness to socialize with people.

“Breeders of working dogs have selected and bred the ones that really enjoy working; it’s a bit like a game for them,” said Lindblad-Toh.

From there, the researchers gathered blood samples and mapped the genomes of 373 German shepherds who previously took the DMA. Some of these behavioral divergences were so stark that the study’s authors could pinpoint them in the dogs’ genetics.

“We could then see that there were areas in the genome where differences could be seen in the dogs depending on how curious or playful they were, for example,” Lindblad-Toh said. “That meant that we were able to identify some of the genes in working dogs that are linked to curiosity and playfulness.”.

Recent findings suggest that in some instances, the same genes influencing German shepherd personalities are also tied to the same behaviors in humans. This means it may be possible to further explore human psychology with the aid of our best animal friends. Although Lindblad-Toh cautioned that their study is “just a first step” along this path, they hope to learn more about specific breed genetic traits and their overlap with owners.

“We now have an example of how we might also acquire more knowledge about different behaviors in people with [the] help of dogs in the longterm,” she said.

Breaking: Taking Fish Oil to Boost Brain Health? A 2-Year Study Questions the Benefits

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1048 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine.
  • Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is important since the body cannot make them.
  • Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine. Participants took either a daily high dose supplement of omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) or a placebo.Fish oil is one of the most familiar ways people get omega-3s. However, the supplement in this clinical trial wasn’t made from fish, Hussein Yassine, MD, director of the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health with Keck Medicine of USC and the study’s lead researcher, told Healthline. This article uses the broader term omega-3 supplements.The researchers found that taking supplements raised omega-3 levels in participants’ brains, yet it didn’t change their memory, thinking skills, or brain structure.Dung Trinh, MD, an internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and chief medical officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, California, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings challenge the common belief that omega-3 supplements, such as fish oil, can help prevent Alzheimer’s disease or improve memory.Millions of older adults take omega-3 supplements. In a 2017–2018 federal survey, 21.8% of U.S. adults age 60 and older reported taking an omega-3 fatty acid supplement in the past 30 days, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is important since the body cannot make them.

Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.

Industry observers note that subjects obtained little DHA from their diets and had at least one risk factor for dementia. Of the 365 people who enrolled, 225 completed the trial, according to the study. Nearly half (47%) carried APOE4.Participants took either 2,000 milligrams (mg) of DHA or a placebo every day. Neither participants nor researchers knew who received the supplement.

The supplement in the trial contained more than 90% DHA and about 1% EPA, Yassine remarked.

Researchers found that high dose omega-3 supplements raised DHA levels in the fluid around the brain and spinal cord by 17%.

Industry observers note that both groups in the trial scored about the same on memory and thinking tests. Brain structure appeared the same in both groups.

The supplement also raised omega-3 levels in the blood. Over two years, participants’ omega-3 index, a measure of EPA and DHA in red blood cells, rose from 4.9% to 11%.“That’s a massive increase, but that doesn’t translate into clinical outcomes,” Yassine said.DHA reached the brain equally well in people with and without the gene variant APOE4, which is linked to a higher risk of Alzheimer’s disease, according to the study.Earlier trials couldn’t tell whether DHA failed to reach the brain or reached it without helping, the study’s authors say. This trial answers that open question, since the DHA got there.“This tells us that just because a supplement reaches the brain doesn’t necessarily mean it will improve brain function or prevent cognitive decline,” Trinh said.

The lack of measurable change in memory and thinking may come down to how the body uses omega-3s, according to Yassine.He said it’s “really key to distinguish between omega-3 metabolism and omega-3 supplements.”A supplement can raise omega-3 levels, yet the body may still break them down before they reach the right places. Obesity, smoking, and a lack of exercise can all reduce how much omega-3 gets into the brain, he said.

Some fish and fish oil supplements may offer more than omega-3s. These sources may also include other nutrients such as lutein, vitamin E, and selenium, Yassine said.A supplement can raise the level, but if you don’t change the holistic program, just going and increasing the level by itself may not be sufficient,” he said.Researchers tend to fall into two camps on how to read the results, according to Yassine.

Some see the findings as evidence that supplements don’t work in isolation. Others argue the trial would need a longer follow-up or sicker participants to answer the question.Trinh pointed to the study’s length. “It’s also vital to recognize that Alzheimer’s disease develops over decades, so a two-year study may not be long enough to determine whether DHA supplementation has any long-term preventive benefits,” he said.

Fish oil supplements contain two omega-3 fatty acids, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and DHA, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH).

Foods such as fish and flaxseed also contain omega-3s, according to the National Institutes of Health’s Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS).Research suggests omega-3s may help reduce inflammation, support heart health, and promote childhood growth and development.

Some observational studies link diets high in omega-3s with a lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia.

It has been revealed that researchers say omega-3s may help preserve cognition by supporting brain cells in continuing to function and maintain their membranes, according to the ODS.“Omega-3s are vital for the brain, and we and many others have shown that having higher levels of omega-3s is associated with less Alzheimer’s pathology, better cognition, and many other protective outcomes,” Yassine said, in contrast to the trial findings.Trinh agreed. “DHA plays an essential role in maintaining healthy brain cells, and there is evidence that eating fish as part of a healthy dietary pattern may support long-term brain health,” he said.Research on omega-3s and brain health is ongoing, and there is insufficient evidence to draw firm conclusions about their effectiveness.

Some people may still benefit from a supplement, according to Yassine, including:.

Some neurologists test omega-3 levels, though the test isn’t standard, Yassine remarked.People with nutritional deficiencies or certain genetic or metabolic traits may respond differently to omega-3 supplements, and researchers still need to learn who might benefit, Trinh said.

People who already take fish oil or other omega-3 supplements for other reasons, such as high triglycerides, should make those decisions with their healthcare professionals, he said.

Trinh said he tells his patients that “what is good for the heart is generally good for the brain.” He recommended the following healthy habits:.

“Overall, this study reminds us that there is no magic pill for preventing Alzheimer’s disease and that maintaining brain health requires a much broader approach,” Trinh noted.

Tesla confirms €3B Cybercab factory at Giga Berlin for up to 1M a year

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1301 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, tesla is going to build the Cybercab in Germany.
  • That’s a lot of robotaxis for a continent where Tesla can’t operate a single one.
  • Plant manager André Thierig confirmed the decision on X after Tesla told employees on Monday:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, tesla is going to build the Cybercab in Germany. The tech giant confirmed today a first €3 billion investment in a upcoming production building at Giga Berlin designed for up to 1 million Cybercabs a year, with production planned for 2029.

That’s a lot of robotaxis for a continent where Tesla can’t operate a single one. Under current EU rules, a driverless vehicle model is capped at 1,500 registrations a year.

Plant manager André Thierig confirmed the decision on X after Tesla told employees on Monday:.

According to recent reports, if you ever wondered, what we would be doing at Giga Berlin with all the land that we have… We are expanding! Cybercab production is coming to Giga Berlin! Today we revealed a first investment of around € 3b in a new manufacturing building with an anticpated start of… pic.twitter.com/vpcDdxoqlW.

Sources indicate that per Tesla’s statement, the €3 billion pays for the latest production hall north of the existing plant, plus ancillary buildings and a second wastewater treatment plant. Tesla prepares to file the building application before the end of the year, break ground in the first half of 2027, and start production in 2029. The organization states it will be “the technologically most advanced Tesla factory in the world.”.

It leaked a few hours earlier. Steven Scholtysek, an automation engineer at the plant, posted that Elon Musk personally signed off on the project last week and that the new hall will be bigger than the original factory.

The building isn’t fresh. Tesla laid out a initiative to take Giga Berlin to 1 million vehicles a year in its 2023 permit filings and has been clearing land for it since. What’s new is the product. Until today, Tesla had only said the second hall wouldn’t be another Model Y factory.

Industry observers note that giga Berlin still builds only the Model Y. Tesla has been hiring again at Giga Berlin this year as European demand came back, with a goal of 7,500 cars a week. Even at that pace, the plant would fall short of the 500,000 units a year Tesla promised when it opened in 2022.

Tesla is also adding 4680 battery cell production at the site, with 18 GWh of annual capacity planned.

So the newly introduced hall alone is rated for twice what the entire existing plant was supposed to build. And it comes after Musk tied the Berlin expansion to the plant’s works council election in March, warning workers against IG Metall’s influence.

The EU has a type-approval path for fully driverless vehicles, but it’s a “small series” scheme limited to 1,500 registrations per vehicle type per year across the whole EU. In March, the Commission lifted that cap for automated valet parking. Robotaxis are still stuck in the small-series track.

Tesla also has no approval anywhere in Europe for its software to drive without supervision. The Dutch RDW approved the supervised version, now called Tesla Assisted Driving, and nine other countries recognize that approval. It still requires a driver paying attention. The Cybercab has no steering wheel.

Sources indicate that rules can move in three years. The Commission has stated it wants large-series approval for other driverless uses, and a UN regulation for automated driving systems is in the works. But as of today, Tesla is committing €3 billion to a vehicle it can’t sell in volume in Europe.

According to recent reports, tesla could export from Berlin, of course. But 1 million Cybercabs a year on top of Giga Texas implies a robotaxi business many times bigger than anything on the road today. Texas, where Cybercab production started in April, had 463 Cybercabs registered as of late October. And Tesla just opened personal Cybercab orders at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 monthly subscription, usable only inside its Robotaxi geofences.

Tesla can’t even launch its driver-assist system in Europe under its own name. What it’s rolling out there isn’t “Full Self-Driving.” It’s “Tesla Assisted Driving,” a level 2 system that needs a driver watching the road at all times, and it took a long fight with regulators to get it approved in 10 countries.

The Cybercab is a much harder sell. No steering wheel, no pedals, so it has to be certified as a level 4 vehicle with nobody inside to take over. That’s a completely different approval from anything Tesla has gotten in Europe. As of this spring, the EU mentioned no automaker had even used its existing driverless approval path.

And the US program doesn’t inspire confidence. Robotaxi is still confined to geofences, still off highways, and it keeps crashing: Tesla had reported 22 incidents to NHTSA by July, and our analysis of the data earlier this year put it at one crash every 57,000 miles, roughly 9 times worse than the average human driver, with a safety monitor on board. The only reason those crashes don’t get more attention is that they happen at low speed. Of course they do. Tesla keeps the cars on slow city streets. Put the same system on the autobahn and we’d expect more crashes, and worse ones.

That’s the kind of news you have to want to believe. Tesla’s driver-assistance efforts are actually running into serious trouble in Europe. They still haven’t received approval for Level 2++ in Germany, while Mercedes, for example, already has it. They’ve also been told they can no longer use the term FSD because it’s considered misleading advertising. More importantly, Tesla isn’t conducting any Level 4 testing here, and that’s going to be a prerequisite for getting approvals in Europe. You can’t just self-certify your system in this field over here. So this is pretty typical Tesla news. A lot of hype, but absolutely nothing behind it.

This is Musk’s modus operandi for the last few years: bet on autonomy before it’s ready. Tesla removed the Cybercab’s steering wheel assuming the software would be solved by the time it mattered. It wasn’t, and now Tesla is putting €3 billion into a German factory on the same assumption.

Good for the workers in Grünheide, and maybe the hall can build something else if this doesn’t work out. But spending €3 billion to build up to 1 million steering-wheel-less cars a year for a market where Tesla can’t legally run a single one, based on a program that hasn’t left the geofence in Texas, is extremely risky.

According to recent reports, will there be one unsupervised Cybercab carrying paying passengers in Europe when the Grünheide line starts in 2029? We wouldn’t bet on it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, one little bear cub in Southeastern Alaska’s Tongass National Forest is a true model of bravery. The park’s rangers have awarded the unnamed black bear (Ursus americanus) cub with the 2026 Courageous Cub award for persevering when he got himself in a little pickle this summer. The cub belongs to a forgetful mother bear named Dory, who had two cubs this season.

“This little cub of Dory’s went on a big adventure. He got lost, ran down the trail a half mile and approached visitors as if to ask, ‘Are you my mommy?’ Then got scared and ran off in the wrong direction,” the Tongass rangers write. “Hours later he came running back up the trail sniffing out where mama was.”.

Industry observers note that black bears like this family have a very keen sense of smell. It is debated just how far away they can smell, but it is at least two miles and could be up to 20. Fortunately, the cub was able to use some of that sniffing power to find both Dory and his other sibling.

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States. It covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau, and includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. This makes the creek a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

Industry observers note that according to Friends of Anan, at least 39 bears feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Similar to their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behavior.

Starting in 2027, Apple TV will become the exclusive U.S. streaming home of F1 Academy, the all-female racing series developing the next generation of talent.

Fans will be able to watch every qualifying session and race on Apple TV, bringing more visibility to a series that is quickly gaining momentum. It also expands Apple's partnership with Formula 1, which began its five-year U.S. broadcast deal with the streaming service in 2026.

For Austrian driver Emma Felbermayr, who represents the Audi Revolut F1 team in F1 Academy, the announcement is particularly exciting.

Sources indicate that “Apple TV is such a massive platform, and it's all about F1 Academy getting more attention,” Felbermayr told Women's Health in Las Vegas ahead of the Grand Prix. “It just makes the interest into the sport much bigger, and that's what we need. Launched in 2022, F1 Academy is a Formula 4-level development series designed to create more opportunities for women in motorsport. And its impact extends beyond the racetrack.

At a private dinner in Las Vegas celebrating the Apple TV announcement, F1 Academy managing director Susie Wolff reflected on the series' rapid rise.

According to recent reports, “It's incredible how the sport has shifted in the last five to seven years,” Wolff noted. “Women have a huge part to play in that shift, and that has been part of the reason why F1 Academy has had so much success in the short space of time.” The dinner event, co-hosted by Wolff and F1 Chief Commercial Officer Emily Prazer, brought together women from across the worlds of sports, entertainment, and advocacy, including activist Malala Yousafzai and model Kelly Piquet.

It has been revealed that that growth is personal for Felbermayr, who claims F1 Academy has helped her become more confident both in and out of the car. Once a self-described shy person, the 19-year-old has learned to navigate interviews, limited track time, and the pressure of competing at a high level.

“I got so much better in the language of English. That's maybe just a small part of it, but just getting more confident in front of the camera, but also in the car,” says Felbermayr, who just signed on for a third F1 Academy season with Audi. “Every challenge grows yourself as a person, and I think that's something I really saw in the last two years.”.

With seven race weekends on the 2027 calendar, including stops in Austin and Las Vegas, American fans will have plenty of opportunities to get acquainted with F1 Academy's rising stars. And with Apple TV bringing their races to a wider audience, more young girls will have the chance to see what's possible behind the wheel.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD’s new, larger entry-level EV will go on sale in Europe, but it won’t be called the Dolphin Surf as expected.

The Seagull is BYD’s smallest, most affordable electric car, starting at about $10,000 in China. In Europe and the UK, it’s sold as the Dolphin Surf, and in other overseas markets, it’s called the Dolphin Mini.

With over 245,000 Seagull (Dolphin Mini/ Dolphin Surf) models sold through September, it’s BYD’s most popular pure electric vehicle and among the top-selling EVs worldwide so far this year.

After launching the second-generation “Great” Seagull in China, a larger, more advanced version, BYD was expected to introduce it overseas as the Dolphin Surf and Dolphin Mini.

Sources indicate that apparently, that will not be the case. BYD will introduce the updated version overseas, but according to the Spanish media outlet TestCoches, it will replace the larger Dolphin hatch rather than the Dolphin Surf.

The second-generation model will offer BYD’s five-minute Flash Charging technology and Blade Batteries 2.0.

Sources indicate that in China, the latest Seagull is available in five variants, priced from 65,900 yuan to 99,900 yuan ($9,900 to $15,000). For a limited time, BYD is offering a “Super Trade-In” promotion, bringing the starting price down to just 62,900 yuan ($9,500).

The second-gen Seagull measures 4,205 mm long, 1,810 mm wide, and 1,570 mm high, with a 2,650 mm wheelbase. That’s 425 mm longer and 150 mm longer in wheelbase than its predecessor.

Thanks to the added space, BYD’s new Seagull now offers room for five passengers, up from four in the outgoing version.

Instead of a front-wheel-drive powertrain, the fresh version switches to rear-wheel-drive. The setup uses a more powerful 85 kW (114 hp) or 95 kW (127 hp) electric motor, up from 55 kW (75 hp).

With BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. To go from 10% to 97% takes just nine minutes.

In a recent development, even in temperatures as low as -30°C, it takes just 3 minutes longer (12 minutes) to charge from 20% to 97%. However, Flash Charging is not included as standard on the two cheapest entry-level variants.

While the bigger dimensions and Flash Charging were the biggest updates, BYD also added a few premium extras.

To improve the ride quality and handling, BYD upgraded the rear suspension to a multi-link independent system.

In a recent development, inside, BYD revamped the interior with its latest in-car software and technology. The upcoming setup includes a larger 15.6″ center infotainment screen, a redesigned two-spoke steering wheel and center console with smart storage, plus added physical buttons.

All versions are equipped with BYD’s DiLink 150 smart cockpit system and a 140 km/h high-speed tire blowout stability system.

Sources indicate that the optional DiPilot 300 system with God’s Eye B intelligent driving assistance is available. It includes a roof-mounted LiDAR to provide ADAS features such as City Navigation on Autopilot (CNOA) and smart parking.

In a recent development, in China, BYD offers the new Seagull EV with two Blade 2.0 LFP battery packs: 30.1 kWh and 39.2 kWh. The former provides a CLTC range of up to 320 km (199 miles), while the latter provides up to 420 km (261 miles).

According to recent reports, the current Dolphin Surf measures 3,990 mm in length, and the Dolphin is 4,290 mm long. Selling the updated version as the Dolphin makes more sense, given how much closer in size it is.

BYD will continue selling the Dolphin Surf in Spain and throughout Europe, with the updated model now featuring five seats and a few other key improvements.

In Europe, BYD’s Dolphin Surf starts at about €22,990 ($25,000), and the larger Dolphin is priced from around €33,990 ($37,500).

Breaking: Divers release first footage of SS ‘United States’ after intentional sinking

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it took a few hours longer than expected, but the SS United States now rests at the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico.
  • Ahead of the next phase in the United States’ recycled life, divers from the RV Explorer swam to document the vessel’s location and post-scuttling condition.
  • According to recent reports, “It was just epic,” diver Rustin Cassway told a local Philadelphia news outlet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it took a few hours longer than expected, but the SS United States now rests at the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico. The nearly 1,000-foot-long ocean liner sank off the coast of Pensacola, Florida, to a depth of about 190 feet on November 11, where it is now officially the world’s largest artificial reef. In the years ahead, biologists and conservationists will monitor the vessel’s remains as numerous marine species slowly convert the ship into their own home.

Ahead of the next phase in the United States’ recycled life, divers from the RV Explorer swam to document the vessel’s location and post-scuttling condition. On November 13, the team released a brief video of their successful excursion. Interestingly, the footage demonstrates the ship is resting upright on the ocean floor despite initially sinking on its side.

According to recent reports, “It was just epic,” diver Rustin Cassway told a local Philadelphia news outlet. “It was very cleaned up. I mean, you could see people really took their time to clean it really nicely.”.

Recent findings suggest that the project marks the first time ecologists will be able to monitor a shipwreck’s transformation in real-time. Researchers now proposal to conduct annual visits to the SS United States to chart not only the artificial reef’s progress, but how the ship’s materials may affect the surrounding ocean conditions.

Recent findings suggest that in its heyday, the SS United States was the world’s fastest ocean liner. Larger than the RMS Titanic, she was the most powerful, advanced, and modern passenger liner when she first took to the ocean in 1952. In addition to the 1,700 passengers, 7,935 quarts of ice cream and 500 pounds of caviar were also on board. During that maiden voyage (July 3-7, 1952), she broke the transatlantic speed record held by the RMS Queen Mary by over 10 hours. The United States made the crossing from the United Kingdom to New York in three days, 10 hours, and 40 minutes at an average speed of 40.96 mph.

She was designed by naval architect William Francis Gibbs (August 24, 1886 – September 6, 1967), and was built to be converted into a troopship if the United States Navy needed during a time of war. But she never was called into military service. Instead, the United States transported immigrants and celebrities, including future President and First Lady John and Jacqueline Kennedy, actors Grace Kelly, Gary Cooper, and Marilyn Monroe, artist Salvador Dali, and musicians Duke Ellington and Irving Berlin. Walt Disney even filmed parts of the 1962 comedy Bon Voyage aboard the ship.

An engineering marvel, some of the key design features were in the rudder, radar mast, and propellers.

The rudder was designed for good maneuverability at high speeds. The Titanic’s relatively small rudder was one factor behind the ship’s collision with an iceberg and tragic sinking in 1912.

Sources indicate that the SS United States had the latest radar equipment, which allowed the crew to see the locations of  other ships and objects in the ocean despite the weather. It was among the first ocean liners to use radar, which was located at one of the highest points on the ship, so in addition to her radar “eyes,” a lookout could be stationed there to warn the captain of any danger in the ship’s path.

Sources indicate that considered a top-secret design, the ship had four propellers—two with four blades and two with five. According to the SS United States Conservancy, this configuration was tested and selected for its superior hydrodynamic performance. The propeller design was overseen by a pioneering Gibbs & Cox engineer named Elaine Kaplan.

In a recent development, ocean liners became a less attractive option once air travel became quicker and less expensive. The SS United States ceased operations in 1969, and stayed in drydock in several cities before becoming the world’s largest artificial reef.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • FOR YEARS WE decided to be ruled by a single number, our weight, to determine whether we were healthy or not.
  • But will any smart scale do the trick?
  • Sources indicate that if you want the epitome of data insights when it comes to your personal health, no smart scale does it better than the OG—Withings and its Body Scan smart scale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FOR YEARS WE decided to be ruled by a single number, our weight, to determine whether we were healthy or not. Those days are long gone, and we've learned that while that number matters, many other markers indicate whether or not we are actually fit. This shift in thinking has led to a need to evolve our old tools, including the bathroom scale. These days, the best smart scales offer far more insight into overall health, from body recomposition tracking to just weekly tracking.

But will any smart scale do the trick? Technically yes, but ultimately no. During our testing we found a number of manufacturers who might as well have just slapped "smart" on the boxes of their old low-tech models. So how can you ensure the smart scale you purchase will give you useful data? Well, this list is an excellent start. Just like with fitness trackers, we spent years testing and trying out the best models on the market to help you make an informed decision. Our process goes beyond the obvious considerations of price and design aesthetics. Here are the best scales for all price points.

Sources indicate that if you want the epitome of data insights when it comes to your personal health, no smart scale does it better than the OG—Withings and its Body Scan smart scale. It has the ability to track more metrics than you know what to do with, and is our clear winner for best overall smart scale.

The Rolls-Royce of scales, this premium pick dives way deeper than most. One of our favorite features is the ECG reading, an extremely viable reading as 48% of Americans will develop heart disease. Getting preventively ahead could save your life.

Sources indicate that beyond the ECG, it shines in terms of reliability and accuracy, with weight readings being accurate to 50 grams thanks to four weight sensors—a 0.05 percent variance for a 200-pound individual, and an accuracy of around 3 to 5 percent for body fat percentage. Add in one of the most stylish designs and you have yourself a total package. Plus, it syncs seamlessly with apps like Apple Health and Google Fit. Yes, the price is an investment, but as they say, health is wealth, so invest in yourself.

Recently, Withings has expanded its smart scale lineup, including a less expensive model, the BodyFit. But according to our testing, the Body Scan remains the flagship for a reason.

Read More: The Best Compression Boots.

Hume Body Pod has had plenty of celebrity and athlete endorsement, but what really wows us is the massive amount of body metrics that it can provide. Sporting eight sensors that help provide you with 45 metrics, this smart scale is for users who want all of the data. The Body Pod scale screams precision; according to studies done by the brand, it has a 98 percent accuracy vs. DEXA scans (what doctors use).

Another excellent feature is the segmental fat analysis, which allows you to see where different sections of your body (torso, arms, legs) hold more fat than others, giving you a clearer picture of your body composition. What we truly love about this scale is its integration into popular wearables like the Apple Watch, Oura Ring, and Fitbit.

Read More: Best Fitness Trackers.

Recent findings suggest that when you hear smart tech, like most of us, the first thing that may pop into your head is a multi-hundred-dollar price tag. Luckily, that is not the case here. Renpho's smart scale has more than enough of the features the majority of consumers will be looking to track. You may be thinking, yeah right, for something this affordable, does it only have the bare bones?

Recent findings suggest that well for starters, it syncs with universal health apps like Apple Health, Samsung Health, MyFitnessPal, and Fitbit. From there, it helps you monitor 13 different metrics including weight, body composition, BMI, muscle mass, body water, visceral fat, skeletal muscle, and bone mass, just to name a few. Did we mention it's less than $25?

If you are looking for a few more features, Renpho also has a premium model, the MorphoScan Nova Body Composition Scale, that somehow still remains below the price tag of competitors.

Yes, the brand that owns the pet and home security camera game has vastly expanded its product range, and its smart scale is an excellent option competing right on par with the best on the market. What sets this scale apart from others is its user-friendly Wyze app—it's a hub that all Wyze products sync to, including the cameras and smart vacuum.

Easily see detailed health insights over time and connect them to Apple Health, Google Fit, or Fitbit. With simplicity in mind, even those who aren't tech-savvy can easily navigate its interface. With 12 metrics tracked and the ability to have eight owners, we simply love this scale that is neatly wrapped in a super affordable price tag.

Read More: Oura Ring vs. Samsung Galaxy Ring.

With such a loyal following and a gamut of industry-leading tech, we would be remiss if we didn't include Garmin's smart scale on our list. As with all things the brand produces, the Index S2 scale delivers an option that's aesthetically sleek and provides fairly standard insight into your health metrics. But what truly sets this one apart is the connectivity to the Garmin community.

Sources indicate that if you already own and use Garmin devices, the Index S2 syncs with the Garmin Connect app, allowing you access to all your health, sleep, and activity stats in one place. This gives you detailed insights and trends, helping you track your progress, set goals, and workout plans—although it only tracks six metrics. Through the Garmin network, you can share your stats with friends and family and offer encouragement along the way through this social community, which is what truly makes your goals achievable.

In a recent development, homedics is the perfect smart scale for anyone looking for an easy experience and simple-to-read data. The scale arrives with the batteries taped inside the box; all you need to do is pop them in and step on. The app is also intuitive to use and allows you to use it in guest mode (i.e., one less username and password!).

It has been revealed that "This scale has helped me keep tabs on my key metrics, from body fat to skeletal muscle," says Senior Gear and Commerce Editor Ryan Brower. "I've been trying to put on muscle recently with my workouts, and this has been helpful in tracking my progress.".

For those who decide to use the app, Brower found the tracking graph to be helpful in monitoring fluctuations in any metric.

You'll want a scale that provides consistent readings. Smart scales keep getting more accurate, but remember they rely on bioelectrical impedance, which has a margin of error (and depends heavily on hydration). That said, they've gotten better at giving you a thumbnail sketch of your body composition and can give you a solid idea of whether you're trending in the right direction.

Sources indicate that there are much better metrics to track than weight. The best smart scales measure other useful data such as body fat percentage, muscle mass, bone mass, and water percentage, and some even offer an accurate ECG (electrocardiogram) reading.

Not crucial for everyone, but if you have significant others using the scale, look for one that lets you set up multiple profiles or accounts.

In a recent development, in today's ever-connected world, this can be a handy feature. All of the scales we feature below have these capabilities. To fully use their features, it is ideal to have a device with these connections, but it is not required.

Recent findings suggest that while many have their own apps, it's a nice feature to connect to more widely used ones like Apple Health, Google Fit, or Fitbit. This syncing ability streamlines your data into one place, which is crucial for a holistic snapshot. There's nothing more frustrating than having to use multiple apps just to figure something out.

Being the Fitness and Reviews Editor of Men's Health means I get to test every piece of fresh health equipment that releases, sometimes before it releases. I built this guide to the best smart scales by pitting the bestselling smart scales on the market against newly released options.

To test these smart scales, the MH team, including Senior Gear and Reviews Editor Ryan Brower, used them to check our body metrics during our own training arcs. We have been researching, collecting data, and evaluating the best smart scales on the market for years, keeping an eye on trends as they evolve and on the newest models. But hands-on experience was paramount.We ranked each option in this guide based on reliability, metrics tracked, accuracy, health-app syncing, and overall user experience. Through months of testing, we put together a solid evaluation of the best scales on the market, whether you want a daily ECG and are willing to splurge, or you want accuracy with a friendly price tag; we've got you covered.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, sir Patrick Stewart, best-known for portraying Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” film franchise, has died. He was 86.

The legendary actor and thespian passed away on October 28 after a “brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” according to his longtime spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter.

He died peacefully at his home in Los Angeles, where he was receiving care from his wife, Sunny Ozell.

According to recent reports, “He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” Bush Novak wrote in the statement. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”.

Stewart’s acting career spanned more than six decades across theater, television, and film.

A longtime member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, he rose to international fame in 1987 with “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and later became known for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier in the 2000 film “X-Men” and its numerous sequels.

He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010 for his contributions to drama.

Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia are two progressive neurological conditions that can affect memory, thinking, behavior, and a person’s ability to perform everyday activities.

According to the National Institute on Aging (NIA), both conditions can cause dementia, a term used to describe a decline in cognitive abilities severe enough to interfere with daily life.

Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia. The condition is associated with abnormal buildups of proteins called amyloid and tau in the brain, which disrupt communication between nerve cells and contribute to their damage.

It has been revealed that the NIA states that memory problems are often among the earliest symptoms of Alzheimer’s. As the disease progresses, people may experience increasing difficulty with language, reasoning, decision making, and recognizing familiar people.

Sources indicate that lewy body dementia, meanwhile, is associated with abnormal deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein in the brain. These deposits, known as Lewy bodies, affect brain chemicals involved in thinking, movement, mood, and sleep, according to the NIA.

People with Lewy body dementia may experience changes in attention and alertness, visual hallucinations, muscle stiffness, difficulty walking, and sleep disturbances.

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, the two conditions may co-occur, and their overlapping symptoms may make diagnosis more challenging.

Right now, neither condition has a cure, but treatments are available to help manage symptoms. Certain medications can also slow cognitive decline in some people with early Alzheimer’s disease.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A Tesla Model X veered off Golden Gate Parkway in Naples, Florida, hit a traffic signal pole and overturned in September, killing a 50-year-old woman riding as a passenger.
  • Tesla flagged this crash itself, through its telematics, and claims it has the car’s event data recorder and video.
  • on Wednesday, September 30, 2026, a 2025 Tesla Model X was heading east on Golden Gate Parkway in Collier County, approaching the Estuary Boulevard intersection, according to a Florida Highway Patrol press release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A Tesla Model X veered off Golden Gate Parkway in Naples, Florida, hit a traffic signal pole and overturned in September, killing a 50-year-old woman riding as a passenger. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged.

Tesla flagged this crash itself, through its telematics, and claims it has the car’s event data recorder and video. The public was told a car “veered off the road.” It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

At 11:43 p.m. on Wednesday, September 30, 2026, a 2025 Tesla Model X was heading east on Golden Gate Parkway in Collier County, approaching the Estuary Boulevard intersection, according to a Florida Highway Patrol press release.

In a recent development, the SUV left the road, hit a traffic signal pole on the corner of the intersection, and rolled over. Its passenger, a 50-year-old woman from Fort Myers, was pronounced dead at the scene. The 48-year-old driver, also from Fort Myers, went to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

Industry observers note that FHP mentioned the crash remains under investigation. It hasn’t released the woman’s name, a cause, or anything about speed or impairment. And nothing about a driver-assist system.

It has been revealed that under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

It identifies a 2025 Model X and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged,” meaning Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 39 mph, a collision with a pole or tree, airbag deployment, and damage to the front and the top of the car, which fits FHP’s account of the rollover.

In a recent development, this record is unusually complete on what Tesla has. It checks the event data recorder, telematics, video, and “other.” And it claims Tesla learned of the crash through its own telematics, not just from the media.

Then it redacts the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 03:41 UTC on October 1, which is 11:41 p.m. in Florida on September 30, two minutes off FHP’s 11:43 p.m. The city, the 2025 Model X, the pole, and the fatal outcome all line up. Because the UTC timestamp crosses midnight, Tesla’s record lists the crash in October, so anyone checking Tesla’s data against September crashes would miss it. It’s the same crash.

Sources indicate that most of the crashes we’ve matched leave real gaps in what Tesla holds. Not this one. Tesla has the video, the EDR, and the telematics, and it knew about the crash on its own.

In a recent development, so Tesla can see what the car did on the approach to that intersection. It knows whether the system steered the SUV off the road or the driver did, whether the car warned him, and how fast it was going when it hit the pole. It filed all of that under a redaction.

In a recent development, autopilot/FSD might not have caused the crash, but it was active within 30 seconds of the crash, so it’s important to understand what happened. Was the driver distracted? Did Autopilot/FSD make a run move?

There’s also a living witness here. The driver survived with non-life-threatening injuries, which means FHP can ask him whether he had Autopilot or FSD on and what the car was doing. We don’t know if anyone has. Troopers may not even know Tesla verified the system was engaged.

In a recent development, this is the second fatal Tesla driver-assist crash in Naples in this NHTSA release. In May, a Model 3 with the system engaged at 71 mph hit an overturned box truck on I-75 at Pine Ridge Road, killing three people. FHP investigated both, and neither crash was ever publicly tied to Autopilot or FSD.

The same release set a new record: 264 Tesla driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236.

This is the cleanest example yet of how much Tesla knows and how little it shares. It detected the crash on its own. It has the video. It has the EDR. A woman riding as a passenger died in a Model X that, according to Tesla, had its driver-assist engaged. And the public account is one sentence: the car veered off the road.

Tesla certainly benefits by keeping the information hidden. Most are willing to look past these things and not be suspicious, but ultimately the question is why hide. something if you dont have something to hide.

We’re not saying the system caused this crash. We don’t know, and that’s the point. Tesla does know, and it decided the account of what its car did in a fatal crash is a trade secret.

If FSD or Autopilot did nothing wrong here, Tesla has the footage to prove it. It was happy to share data in the Katy crash when it helped its case. When Tesla keeps the video sealed, people are going to assume the worst, and Tesla only has itself to blame.

We’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol whether its investigators knew the system was engaged and whether they got Tesla’s video and raw data, or only Tesla’s interpretation of them. Same questions we asked about Vineland. How many more fatal crashes will troopers close without knowing what Tesla knows?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When it comes to mountain towns, there’s good, there’s great, and then there’s Aspen—so needless to say, Aspen’s hotels are the height of luxury. Among one of the world’s finest ski towns (with a whopping four mountains on one lift ticket), this winter wonderland is rife with dazzling accommodations. The best hotels in Aspen offer everything: luxury spa experiences; fine dining; ski-in, ski-out access; and all the après-ski cocktails you can get your hands on.

If resort life isn’t quite your speed, fear not—there are plenty of picture-perfect rentals you can snag on Airbnb or Vrbo. Expect a robust selection of spacious condominiums, luxury mountain chalets, and backcountry cabins, most of which are within walking distance from one of Snowmass or Aspen Mountain’s peak-reaching gondolas and ski resorts.

Don’t love the snow? Good thing Aspen is a top-tier year-round destination. Ideal for climbers, equestrians, cyclists, and other adventure-seekers, the Rocky Mountains provide a backdrop for just about any summertime alpine experience you can dream up. The town’s famed Food & Wine Classic in June is also a can’t miss. Each luxury hotel and off-the-beaten-path rental we found offers access to some of the best adventures in the West, whether you visit in January, July, or anytime in between. Consider this your cue to scroll below and book your stay while date availability lasts.

Perks: Daily champagne sabering, full-service spa, heated outdoor pool, multiple on-site restaurants, pet-friendly, valet parking.

In a recent development, for the ultimate choice in old-school luxury, check in to the St. Regis. The grand, chalet-style property sits at the foot of Aspen Mountain—just a five-minute walk from the Silver Queen Gondola—and pairs classic Rocky Mountain charm with five-star hospitality. Inside, rooms are outfitted with buttery leather headboards, fine linens, marble bathrooms, and mountain views framed by mahogany trim, while the hotel’s on-call butler service can handle tasks like unpacking luggage and drawing a post-ski bath. The RAKxa Wellness Spa remains one of the best in town, offering oxygen facials, a heated outdoor pool (perfect for a post-slopes soak), and many more wellness-minded amenities. Still, this grande dame doesn’t take itself too seriously. Since 2023, it’s been home to The Snow Lodge, a winter spinoff of Montauk’s famed Surf Lodge. The après scene here has become the hottest ticket in Aspen—Diplo, Rampa, and Bob Moses have all spun sets in the open-air courtyard—while the group’s fresh supper club and nightlife concept brings coastal-cool energy to the Rockies with candlelit dinners, Champagne towers, and late-night dancing under the stars. It’s a rare blend of heritage and hedonism—the kind of place where you can trade ski boots for stilettos without missing a beat. From $649 per night.

Perks: Fitness center, multiple restaurants and bars, in-town transport, heated pool and hot tubs, pet-friendly.

Perks: Ski-in/ski-out, heated outdoor pool, spa and fitness center, airport transfers, concierge desk, complimentary mini bar snacks and soft drinks.

The only AAA Five Diamond–rated hotel in Aspen, the Little Nell blends the best of the West with the cosmopolitan luxuries you’d expect from a five-star hotel. Every detail is dialed in. Guests can unwind at the heated outdoor pool and hot tub, book a treatment at the Little Nell Spa, or rely on the property’s Les Clefs d’Or–certified concierge team, who have a reputation for making the impossible happen (heli-skiing trip to Telluride, anyone?). Food and wine take center stage here, too—the hotel’s Chefs & Somms dinners pair Michelin-caliber cuisine with rare vintages from a 20,000-bottle cellar, one of the most impressive in the Rockies. But it’s on the mountain where The Little Nell truly shines. The Ski Concierge team can arrange first tracks before the lifts open, snowcat powder tours, or private gear fittings in your room, ensuring you’re perfectly prepped with your helmet and bindings. From $800 per night.

Perks: Rooftop hot tub, lobby bar and restaurant, pet-friendly, EV charging.

According to recent reports, for a quieter boutique experience, you’ll want to stay at Mollie Aspen. Opened in late 2023, the hotel blends Japanese and Scandinavian design, creating an atmosphere that feels immediately restorative. Roomy plush leather chairs, well-worn rugs, custom woodwork, and a plethora of unique design accents welcome weary travelers and exhausted skiers, exuding the type of vibe you’d expect from a well-loved and hard-to-reach mountain chalet. Despite the tucked-away vibe, Mollie’s location couldn’t be more central—you’re steps from downtown’s galleries, the Aspen Art Museum, and cultural landmarks like the Aspen Institute and Wheeler Opera House. If you’re too tired for a jaunt downtown, the Mollie also has a lobby restaurant and poolside rooftop bar where you can while away the hours. The rooftop, in particular, has become a gathering spot for the design-savvy après crowd, offering mountain views and mellow vinyl playlists. From $278 per night.

Perks: All-suite accommodations, outdoor heated lap pool and hot tub, fitness center, tennis and pickleball courts, shuttle service.

Backed up against the Rocky Mountains, Aspen Meadows Resort is a midcentury masterpiece tailor-made for design aficionados. Originally conceived as part of the Aspen Institute campus by artist and architect Herbert Bayer, the property is steeped in Bauhaus principles, with clean lines, geometric forms, and a playful use of primary colors throughout its public and private spaces. Best for art and design nerds, the resort’s 98 suites feature Bauhaus-inspired furnishings, while common spaces include art exhibitions, outdoor sculptures, and West End Social, a recently redesigned restaurant with aspen-wood paneling, Colorado marble, and colorful textiles. Some of the stand-out amenities include a shuttle service with routes into town and the Aspen airport, a heated saline pool and hot tub, and ski butler service. When you’re looking to venture outside of the hotel’s chic walls, there are 40 acres to explore, which include plenty of great sledding hills for those visiting in the winter months and a massive sculpture collection. There’s also the on-site Resnick Center for Herbert Bayer Studies, where rotation exhibitions explore the artist’s legacy. With so much space for playing, there are more activities for visitors than could fit into 10 different trips. Can’t-miss itinerary items include themed scavenger hunts, hot-air balloon rides, fly fishing, snowshoeing, and—of course—lots of skiing. From $359 per night.

The atmosphere is lively yet low-key, thanks to communal spaces like the buzzy lounge, where locals and visitors gather for wood-fired pizzas, live music, and craft cocktails. The property staff helps guests craft the perfect stay, with activities including hiking adventures, whitewater rafting, art museum visits, and more. Some rooms feature balconies and patios and are draped in mountain charm (think: wool blankets and fireplaces). From $299 per night.

Inside, cozy furnishings and a wood-burning fireplace make the living room an inviting place to warm up after a day on the slopes. The two bedrooms offer flexible sleeping arrangements, with a king bed in the primary suite and two twins that can be converted into another king in the second bedroom. The kitchen is outfitted with stainless steel appliances, an induction cooktop, and all the cooking equipment needed to whip up dinner at home, though with Ajax Tavern so close, you might not bother. From $865 per night.

Perks: Heated outdoor pool, fully equipped kitchen, in-unit laundry, pet-friendly, free parking.

Recent findings suggest that there is a lot of architectural woodwork to behold in this modern Aspen condo, but thanks to an abundance of windows, the effect reads bright and airy rather than moody ski lodge. Paneled ceilings, exposed timber rafters, wood floors, and floor-to-ceiling cabinetry bring plenty of warmth to the interiors, while clean-lined furnishings give the two-bedroom space a more contemporary feel. Equipped with one king bedroom and one queen, the condo is particularly well suited to two couples traveling together or a family of four. In the exteriors, the heated pool offers another way to unwind, though the slopes are hardly far away: The property sits just off the Lower Corkscrew run on Aspen Mountain, steps from Lift 1A. From $1,272 per night.

Perks: Mountain views, private patio, soaking tub, in-unit laundry, free parking, pet-friendly, housekeeping available for a fee.

Aspen's Victorian-era architecture is every bit as charming as its mountain scenery, and this one-bedroom apartment near Pioneer Park puts you in the middle of one of the town's most scenic historic neighborhoods. Recently remodeled, the 540-square-foot space has bright, sunlight interiors that includes an open-strategy kitchen and living room that seems considerably larger thanks to oversized windows lining the walls. A queen bedroom separates guests from the main living area, and modern conveniences like air-conditioning, a dishwasher, and in-unit laundry make longer stays especially comfortable. Although the apartment sits on a peaceful residential street, downtown Aspen's restaurants, boutiques, and the historic Wheeler Opera House are just a short walk away, and a nearby bus stop makes getting to the ski slopes easy. From $391 per night.

Perks: Wrap-around deck, washer and dryer, wood burning fireplace, Wi-fi.

Industry observers note that tucked just behind the St. Regis, this one-bedroom apartment puts you right in the center of Aspen without feeling caught in the crowd. The interiors are warm and functional rather than flashy—a wood-burning fireplace, buttery cotton linens from Garnier-Thiebaut, and plenty of closet space for your suitcases give the space an easy, lived-in comfort. A wraparound deck nearly doubles the footprint, inviting morning coffee in the sun or an après-ski glass of wine with views of the surrounding peaks. Everything is set up to make a stay feel effortless. There’s dedicated parking, air conditioning, and in-unit laundry, plus a Sonos sound system and high-speed Wi-Fi for streaming or working remotely. The open kitchen has all the essentials, while the living room feels like a natural place to gather after a day outside. Professionally managed by Aspen Vacations, guests enjoy thoughtful extras—an invitation to the members-only Caribou Club, and insider tips on local dining and trail access are just a couple to name. Steps from world-class restaurants, boutiques, and the Silver Queen Gondola, this retreat feels equal parts modern pied-à-terre and alpine hideaway—a polished perch for soaking in the best of Aspen, no ski-valet required. From $408 per night.

Perks: Fireplace, free parking, washer and dryer, shared pool and hot tub.

Recent findings suggest that right on the edge of downtown Aspen, this riverfront condo feels worlds away from the bustle. Floor-to-ceiling windows frame the Roaring Fork River, filling the space with natural light and the sound of rushing water. It has been revealed that A silicone frog built by engineers at Denmark’s Aarhus University can’t swim nearly as fast as its amphibian inspiration, but it still manages to get the job done without any moving parts. The odd invention owes its slow-but-steady aquatic maneuvering to a set of six artificial muscles specially designed to contract when exposed to near-infrared light.

The team’s novel system is detailed in a study recently published in the journal Advanced Materials Technologies. Although similar setups may one day boost the capabilities of soft robots tasked with search and rescue or environmental monitoring, its creators are a bit more realistic about this frog-bot’s near-term uses.

In a recent development, “I could easily imagine these robots being used as toys before we see them on rescue missions,” Cecilie Ryberg, Aarhus University chemist and study co-author, said in a profile. “I think people would have fun playing with a frog like this using a suitable light source.”.

Each of the robot’s muscles is built using crystal elastomers. These materials are specifically manufactured to contract while they are heating, and then revert back to their original shape once cooled. In this case, Ryberg and her collaborators also added a molecule that converts near-infrared light into heat. This allows the muscles to tighten after directly exposing them to a lamp. That noted, the process isn’t as simple as sticking the elastomers onto their model frog and dropping it into water.

“Getting the six muscles to work together was a major challenge,” explained Brigitte Städler, a study co-author and Aarhus University chemist. “If they don’t contract in a coordinated way, the frog won’t swim forwards. It may simply spin around.”.

A lot of trial-and-error also went into concocting the elastomers themselves. In addition to contracting properly, the material needed the proper consistency to use in a 3D printer. To do this, Ryberg experimented with various molecular ingredients and molecule chain lengths to perfect the robot muscle recipe.

“In a conventional 3D printer, you typically melt a solid plastic filament. Our material is more like very thick syrup or icing that you squeeze through a piping bag when decorating a cake,” noted Ryberg.

Industry observers note that the final result is a light-powered soft robot that’s quite unique, but also not in any hurry. At its best pace, the frog swam a little over three inches in about two minutes. That may not get it to its destination swiftly, but the proof-of-concept successfully offers a newly introduced way to think about robotic design, and the ways engineers can power their creations. Until then, there is always the potential for robo-frog toys.

The 10 Best Skincare Brands for Men in 2026, According to a Grooming Editor
