⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • I REMEMBER being about 10 years old and spending hours in my grandmother’s product-strewn bathroom.
  • It has been revealed that I was transfixed by the ritual of it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I REMEMBER being about 10 years old and spending hours in my grandmother’s product-strewn bathroom. In the middle of her pink-tiled bathroom was a small alcove with a skirted makeup table. Perched on top were probably a dozen, maybe more, intricately detailed glass perfume bottles and coordinating scented powders. The fragranced dusting powders were applied with oversized, almost-feathery puffs to absorb oil from the skin and leave it smelling fresh and clean, while the perfume itself acted like a topper, locking in the coordinating scent.

It has been revealed that I was transfixed by the ritual of it. Scent has always had an emotional lure of sorts. Whether it transports you back in time or conjures a mood, the connections that fragrances evoke are personal and emotional. All that unfolds once a fragrance makes contact with the skin. As the notes dance and bloom, the scent really takes hold. But what if the skin-scent connection went one step further? Could a fragrance improve the tone, texture, quality, and health of our skin?

It’s no longer a theoretical—it’s reality.

It has been revealed that dual-purpose beauty products used to be a one-off. Nowadays, it’s expected that a product will tackle two concerns at once. “We’ve already seen growing interest in functional fragrances, scents formulated with sensitive skin in mind, and alternative fragrance formats like hair mists and body oils, so it’s not surprising to see brands exploring ways to incorporate skincare ingredients into traditional fragrance formats,” notes Darryl Do, a senior perfumer and fragrance expert at Delbia Do Fragrance & Flavors. The idea of perfume that offers skincare benefits is fitting, and, quite honestly, maybe even a little late to the game. “It feels relevant as consumers become more conscious of the ingredients in their beauty products and what they intend to deliver,” Do continues.

Meet the experts: Darryl Do is a senior perfumer and fragrance expert at Delbia Do Fragrance & Flavors. Jenna Queller, MD, is a dermatologist and founder of DermWorks in Boca Raton. Charlene Valledor is a cosmetic chemist and the co-founder and president of SOS Beauty. Farah K. Ahmed is president and CEO of the fragrance creators association (FCA).

As skincare and scent merges into a brand-newly introduced category, some are wondering what took so long. “Scent has long been part of wellness rituals,” states Farah K. Ahmed, President & CEO Fragrance Creators Association (FCA). “What’s different today is that we have science showing that functional fragrances actually work.” We spoke with scent experts and a cosmetic chemist for the backstory on the trend and how to make the most of fragrances infused with skincare so you can reap the benefits.

Skin and scent have a long-standing connection. “In the fragrance industry, the term “skin scent” describes fragrances that are close to the natural scent of skin in order to complement it rather than overpower it,” says Do. But how a scent wears on the skin varies.

Recent findings suggest that it’s all comes down to body chemistry, which includes pH, how much natural oil is produced by your skin, moisture and perspiration levels, and natural odor, explains Charlene Valledor, a cosmetic chemist and the co-founder and president of SOS Beauty. That’s why the very same perfume can smell wildly different from one person to the next. Someone with a skin pH of 5.75, more sebum, or who eats a spicy diet, for example, will provide a different environment than someone with a skin pH of 4.75, drier skin, and eats virtually no spicy foods.

Sources indicate that but it doesn’t stop there: What you apply to your skin before perfume also influences how a fragrance takes hold. By the time most people finish their morning routine, they’ve already created a fragrance profile and applying perfume introduces another layer on top of that existing baseline, Do indicates.

Unfortunately, your skin doesn’t always play nicely with certain scents. The ingredients in the bottle themselves, which includes everything from the concentration of alcohol to the presence of essential oils can cause itching, redness, and general irritation. “Fragrance can directly disrupt skin’s protective barrier or trigger an outright allergic reaction,” explains board-certified dermatologist Jenna Queller, MD, founder of DermWorks in Boca Raton, FL. “Irritation can happen to anyone, particularly when the skin is already dry or compromised. An allergy is different: the immune system has become sensitized to a specific ingredient.”.

Dr. Queller states that while certain compounds like cinnamal, eugenol, isoeugenol, and geraniol are well-known contact allergens and can damage or irritate the outer layer of skin and weaken the protective barrier, others, such as limonene and linalool, which are commonly found in citrus, floral, and herbal fragrances, can become more allergenic after exposure to air. “A higher concentrations can increase the risk of irritation,” she says. “However, no single concentration guarantees a product is safe for everyone. If you develop a true allergy, even a small amount can trigger a reaction.”.

Industry observers note that deciphering how much allergen is in a perfume—even in a natural or organic scent or essential oil, which isn’t necessarily a safe option for sensitive skin—is difficult. “You can’t judge a fragrance by how strong it smells,” Dr. Queller suggests. “Subtle scents can contain allergens, which is why the ingredient list matters more than the intensity.” If your skin is sensitive or dry, or you are rosacea- or eczema-prone, a fragrance intolerance or allergy, which often manifests as redness, itching, dryness, burning, and even swelling, hives, or blisters, is likely to form more easily, especially since she says the skin barrier may already be impaired.

So, what’s the best way to wear a fragrance while also safeguarding your skin’s health, especially if one of the trendier skincare-infused fragrances may not be a good fit? Dr. Queller suggests applying the scent to clothing rather than directly to the skin, although she says it’s not a guarantee because fragrance can transfer to the skin. Of course, each scents’ chemical composition can vary so naturally, a bit of trial and error may be involved to determine which irritate you specifically.

Recent findings suggest that the latest fragrance technology is innovative because it not only helps you avoid irritant reactions, it promises to care for a nurture skin directly. In fact, it seems we’re moving toward a world in which dual-purpose fragrances can leave you smelling good and feeling soft. It makes sense when you learn that keratinocytes—the primary cells in your epidermis—contain olfactory receptors that respond to certain fragrances, indicates Dr. Queller. “Skin has its own sensory biology,” she says, “and research suggests scent may influence key cellular functions, including skin regeneration and wound healing.” In fact, one study showed that Sandalore, a sandalwood note, activates a receptor that speeds up cell growth and migration to help close cuts and sores. Another research paper found that the same pathway prolonged the growth phase of cultured human hair follicles.

Industry observers note that it’s a welcome development. We all live extremely busy, over-scheduled lives and most of us want beauty products that do more than one thing. The latest Nakery Beauty Skin + Hair Exosome Perfume captures this ethos brilliantly. It combines plant-derived exosomes, thought to boost collagen, reduce inflammation, and support healthier-looking skin, with one of two scents: a warm blend of vanilla, amber, and almond or an oceanic mix of sheer musk, sea air notes, and driftwood. Similarly, Bella Hadid’s alcohol-free, essential oil-powered Orebella collection promises to hydrate skin with a bi-phase formula that simultaneously moisturizes while delivering a long-lasting scent. Another offering worth noting is Salt + Stone’s Body Mist. In six intoxicating scents, each light-as-air-mist is infused with glycerin and red algae for smooth, touchable skin. The idea of all of these is that rather than leaving your outer layer dehydrated and more susceptible to aging—a common complaint with scents formulated with alcohol—these products support dry skin and enhance its moisture levels.

Future Society’s unscented Base Scent follows a similar path in a different way. It works with the skin’s natural microbiome to help the body smell better. It relies on aspergillus ferment, zinc, and arginine, and you can wear it on its own or layer it over perfume to create a more neutral body scent over time. The microbiome also factors significantly into Argentum’s Les Perfumes Infinis collection. Water-based and free of potentially drying alcohol, each of the twelve scents is formulated in such a way as to not disrupt the delicate balance of bacteria naturally found on your outer layer.

Nakery Beauty Skin + Hair Exosome Perfume.

This fragrance, proven to last up to twelve hours, harnesses the power of plant-derived exosomes and an advanced hydration complex to hydrate skin and strengthen its barrier.

All of Orebella’s scents, including this brand-new blend of creamy milk, woody amber, and fresh bergamot features a base of hydrating snow mushroom and the brand’s signature five-oil blend.

Salt & Stone Bergamot & Hinoki Body and Hair Fragrance Mist.

Salt + Stone’s body products have rightfully gained a cult following and their hair & body mists are no different. What does make them different is that they contain humectant glycerin to help skin hang onto moisture and red algae to promote smoothness. This bergamot and hinoki blend is one of their latest.

Sources indicate that A scent with no scent? Yup. This one is formulated with prebiotics that work with your skin’s natural microbiome to keep your natural scent more consistent and balanced.

ARgENTUM Les Parfums Infinis LOVER Eau de Parfum.

Sources indicate that each of these alcohol- and solvent-free fragrances is gentle on skin and blended based upon one of the main elements (Earth, Air, Water). Lover, for example, is a mix of geranium, rose, and berries meant to evoke a garden after a rainfall.

Sources indicate that so, can a few spritzes of a skin-boosting fragrance achieve the same goals as a watery serum or thicker moisturizer? Potentially, but as Dr. Queller shares, it really comes down to the formulation. “A fragrance that incorporates ingredients like hyaluronic acid, glycerin, ceramides, or nourishing emollients can help improve skin hydration and support the skin barrier.” Her advice? Look beyond the label and marketing claims. “A beautifully formulated fragrance can offer skincare benefits, but that doesn’t automatically make it suitable for sensitive skin.”.

Recent findings suggest that what is undoubtedly true is that the skin-scent connection remains strong, perhaps stronger than ever, and this new fragrance category may provide more options for those who may not have been able to wear scent before. These next-generation fragrances go one step further than functional fragrances, which can boost your mood, productivity, and wellness, to focus on skin health in a way that was never tackled before. So go ahead and douse yourself in one of these new skin health-boosting fragrances and wait for everyone to ask, “What perfume are you wearing?”.

Elise rose the ranks at NewBeauty magazine from an editorial assistant to Executive Beauty Editor, overseeing and reporting on all things beauty, plastic surgery, anti-aging, health, and wellness.

She has been featured on Extra TV, WPTV, and WPLG, on satellite tours, and as a featured expert in Perricone MD infomercials. She also runs the Gen Z skincare brand, TWiiSH, with her teenage daughter, Madysen.

Underwood previously served as beauty and wellness director at Oprah Daily and O, The Oprah Magazine. During his tenure leading beauty content for the Oprah brand at Hearst, stories Underwood commissioned were awarded the Skin Cancer Foundation Media Award and a Fragrance Award for Editorial Excellence (his second). He was the launch Beauty Director of Dr. Oz THE GOOD LIFE, and has held additional editorial positions at Fitness, Organic Style, Good Housekeeping, Life & Style Weekly, and Woman’s Day and has written for Self, Shape, Seventeen, Redbook, Cosmopolitan, and many more. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

In a recent development, BACK PAIN DOESN'T care about your big intends to sail through life in comfort, making it hard to do everything from getting in a workout to sitting at your computer. Relief can come in many forms, including regularly stretching and strengthening the surrounding muscles, but sometimes, it can also involve using one of the best inversion tables to ease pressure on your back.

“An inversion table is a device that allows you to hang at an angle, or even upside down, with your feet secured,” explains Max Shlykov, MD, an orthopedic spine surgeon at the Maryland Spine Center. “This position stretches and decompresses the spine and surrounding muscles.”.

It has been revealed that it’s notable to get this out of the way now: An inversion table won’t magically cure your back pain or fix the underlying cause of it. But it can temporarily ease your pain and the tension that’s contributing to it. Inversion tables tend to be especially helpful for people with chronic back concerns like herniated discs, sciatica, degenerative disc disease, muscle spasms, or general stiffness, according to Shayan Ghadamabadi, DPT, a physical therapist at Michigan State University Health Care Physical & Occupational Therapy.

The best inversion tables are sturdy enough to support your height and weight, with adjustable hanging angles, Dr. Shlykov says. “Models that are more lightweight may be easier on your back to use and set up,” he adds.

You’re not born knowing how to pick an inversion table, making it key to choose wisely. Here’s what to consider when looking for one of these pain-relieving tools, plus sturdy options to try. Because you need to know how to actually use one of these tables, we included advice for beginners to help put you on the right path to greater comfort.

Teeter’s FitSpine X3 Inversion Table hits all our best marks thanks to its durability, extended ankle lock handles, and secure, comfortable fit. The device is made with heat-treated steel for unmatched strength and support, and the foam backrest prevents your body from slipping or sliding while inverted, according to Dr. Wallace.

Sources indicate that the comfortable table is lined with acupressure nodes to target and release trigger points, and Dr. Wallace indicates the FlexTech bed moves with your body to enhance decompression and improve range of motion. You can also rest assured about safety features, as the patented wrap-around ankle cups are secure and supportive. Dr. Mesiwala says this is crucial for proper relaxation and effectiveness. What’s more, the lumbar bridge can help release lower back tension and alleviate glute pain triggered by sciatica.

According to recent reports, you’ll also get access to a free personal training app with a library of video and audio guides for on and off the inversion table, Dr. Verma claims. The only qualm? It may be difficult or time-consuming to assemble.

Read More: The Best Compression Boots, Tested By Us.

The Innova ITX9900 Heavy Duty Inversion Therapy Table is a budget-friendly option that doesn’t compromise on quality, according to Dr. Wallace. It offers a six-position adjustable pin system for safety locking and consistent inversion, a large, padded backrest, and soft-touch foam handlebars for easy access to getting in and out of position, he claims. This table is great for anyone, but it’s particularly good for beginners thanks to its ease of use and adjustable headrest, height, and footrest.

Sources indicate that this inversion table also features a True Balance System, which helps customers find their center of gravity for smooth, seamless inversion. Not only will this maximize tension release, but it can also improve spinal decompression. Another pro: The headrest is adjustable, too.

In a recent development, when it comes to getting a full, comfortable stretch, the EP-560 is a safe bet. It features patented wrap-around ankle supports, an ergonomic T-grip ankle lock, and an easy-dial foot platform for a more comfortable, secure fit. The backrest is also a game-changer. Most inversion tables use a simple foam material; the EP-560 ComforTrak backrest is designed to reduce friction and enhance spinal stretch and decompression. We also love that it’s pretty customizable. It comes with built-in tools for easy adjustability, including a Lumbar Bridge for deeper traction on the lower back and Acupressure Nodes that target muscle tension.

Sources indicate that the device is made out of an ultra-durable, heat-treated steel, adding an extra layer of strength and support. If you’re a little closer to the 300-lb range, this is a solid option.

Recent findings suggest that it’s on the pricier side, but the Harison Electric Inversion Table is a top pick for both Dr. Mesiwala and Dr. Verma thanks to its adjustable footbed, memory-foam backrest, and heavy-duty build. The device is made with seamless welding and a steel frame to support up to 350 pounds, and the ergonomic ankle lock design is supportive without feeling too tight or restrictive. Security is also a top priority, and the table includes a high-quality safety belt that allows you to strap in while inverted (on top of the secure ankle holders).

The table is heavier than other options on this list, but it’s foldable for easy storage. It also includes a 30-day trial and replacement of spare parts within one year for no extra cost.

Read More: The Best Massage Guns, Tested By Us.

If you’re looking for an inversion table that doubles as a massager, here’s your pick. The vertical massage pad covers the entire spine with a contoured lumbar pad for a close-up massage and vibrating sensation, and the in-unit heating pad provides warmth to the lower back. There are also multiple mode settings to suit your massage and heat preferences, and the included user manual provides all necessary instructions and details.

Industry observers note that this model has a latest, improved ankle-holding system to reduce pressure on the ankles when inverted, while still ensuring a secure, protective fit. There’s also a six-position pin system on the side of the machine that lets you adjust the angle without dismounting the device.

In a recent development, each inversion table accommodates different heights, so it's key to read the fine print. The Teclor Inversion Table adjusts to fit people up to 6'8", making it a good option for taller consumers. It also can support up to 350 pounds, one of the largest weight capacities you’ll find.

This is a relatively simple inversion table, and the low price supports that. But you’ll still get a comfortably padded back, cushioned handles, and an easy-to-reach handle for adjustability. The ankle-holding system is thickly padded, too. A double-locking system helps to ensure your device is firmly in place when it’s in use. When you’re done inverting, it folds up small enough to stash in a closet.

Read More: The 6 Best Compression Boots to Support Muscle Recovery.

Consider the Teeter FitSpine LX9 the slightly more luxurious version of our top pick, the X3. This has all the elements users love about the X3, including that durable heat-treated steel frame and padded back, but in a slightly sleeker, user-friendly design. The LX9 has an eight-point floating suspension system for a large range of motion, along with reinforced padded handles for a comfortable grip.

According to recent reports, enjoy eight acupressure nodes to help relieve muscle tension while you hang. The included lumbar bridge is adjustable and works to tweak your hip alignment. The LX9 has a step-through design with a specialized boarding platform to make it easy to get on and off. There’s even a built-in storage caddy to hold your gear while you invert.

Using an inversion table isn’t as simple as diving into a latest set of dumbbells. These devices require you to move your body upside-down, making it important to know what you’re doing and how to ease into the process.

It’s key to start with a “modest” angle vs. going into a full-out inversion when you’re starting out, according to Raymond Agostino, DPT, owner of Agostino Athletics in Fort Myers, Florida. “The goal is to introduce your body to the position and create a gentle traction effect without overwhelming your system,” he indicates.

In a recent development, agostino suggests starting with a gentle recline, like 20 to 25 degrees for 30 to 45 seconds and see how you feel. “If you feel comfortable and don't experience dizziness, increased pain, or other symptoms, you can gradually increase the time or angle over future sessions,” he says. Agostino recommends only changing one variable at a time—angle and inversion time—to ease yourself in. “You don't need to go farther upside down and stay there longer all at once,” he says.

According to recent reports, when you’re inverted, you may feel a pressure sensation in your head or a mild “head rush,” Agostino notes. “When your head is positioned below your heart, blood pressure and pressure within the eyes can increase, which is one reason inversion feels very different from simply lying flat,” he explains. You might also feel a feeling of fullness in your head or facial pressure. “Those sensations should remain mild and should resolve when you return upright,” according to Agostino.

It has been revealed that agostino points out that you don’t get a trophy for going completely upside down. “If a smaller angle provides the stretch or relief you're looking for, there may be no reason to progress to a full inversion,” he indicates.

Safety is paramount when shopping for an inversion table. "It’s ideal to find a product with comfortable ankle straps and safety locks to keep you secure and in place," says Kushagra Verma, MD, a board-certified orthopedic spine surgeon at DISC Sports and Spine Center. You also want to make sure the table can be controlled and manipulated by the user if you blueprint to use the device alone. Inversion tables should be used with caution, especially if you’re a beginner, says Rahul Shah, MD, a board-certified orthopedic spine and neck surgeon at Premier Orthopaedic Associates. Additionally, older adults and those who have chronic dizziness, high blood pressure, glaucoma, inner ear problems, heart disease, and/or severe injuries should avoid inversion tables without talking to their doctor first, he says. Keep this in mind, too, per Agostino: “A little pressure may be expected. Feeling like something is wrong is not something you need to train yourself to tolerate.” If it feels like your back pain is worsening, or if you develop new numbness, tingling, weakness, or radiating pain, Agostino recommends that you stop using the inversion tale.

Sturdiness and durability are crucial for preventing accidents or instability while you’re upside down, Dr. Verma says. He recommends always looking for a product made with high-quality materials, such as stainless steel, to provide better support and longevity. Be sure to read customer reviews and seek expert opinions on the machine's sturdiness when shopping. Of course, all the selections on our list have been vetted in this way.

In addition to safety features, all experts agree that it’s crucial to consider how much weight an inversion table can safely hold. (The machine should clearly state this in the product description.) Because the machine puts you in a rather compromising position, maximum weight capacity is key for keeping you safe and at ease, Dr. Shah says. Going over the weight capacity raises the odds that the table will break or flip while you’re on it, potentially injuring you in the process, Agostino says.

It has been revealed that it’s vital to consider the table's length to ensure it accommodates your size and height, says Ali Mesiwala, MD, a neurosurgeon and complex spine expert at DISC Sports and Spine Center. Most inversion tables are adjustable for a customized fit, but it’s best to ensure the maximum height is within your range for effective use. The width of the table is another key factor, as a wider table can offer more stability during inversion, particularly if you’re on the taller or heavier side, says Brian Wallace, DC, a chiropractor at Pinewood Family Care. As a general rule of thumb, the width of the table should be wide enough for your core to conformably fit and not fall to either side, Dr. Shah adds.

According to recent reports, depending on your needs, different inversion tables include add-on features like lumbar spine support, heat, memory foam, or massage elements, Dr. Wallace says. These extra features are not a necessity, but they can be beneficial if you’re looking for added comfort and therapeutic benefits, he says. Just remember: extra add-ons should be considered second to the table's fundamental stability, comfort, and safety.

An inversion table isn’t the cheapest tool you’ll use to reduce your back pain, but there is a range to consider. Most tables will run you anywhere from $150 to $450, with higher-priced models having additional features like heat, memory foam, and massage.

To track down the best inversion tables, Men’s Health editors, including contributor Korin Miller, consulted three orthopedic surgeons, a neurosurgeon, a chiropractor, and two physical therapists to learn more about the notable features to look for in an inversion table. From there, we looked at the most popular inversion tables on the market and narrowed the field based on our experts’ requirements. Each inversion table was ranked based on factors such as size, weight capacity, and safety features. This story was first published in August, and was updated in November to reflect the most recent products on the market, along with advice on how to use these machines.

Extended inversion can cause excessive blood flow to the head and lead to nausea, vomiting, and dizziness, so Dr. Mesiwala recommends using an inversion table for a maximum of five minutes at a time, up to twice a day. If you’re a beginner, he suggests only inverting for 30 seconds once a day as you get your bearings.

Recent findings suggest that the best time to use an inversion table is typically when your muscles are relaxed, such as after a workout at the end of the day, notes Dr. Wallace. Remember: You should not be inverted for long periods, and it’s best to start slowly and work your way up to time and frequency.

According to recent reports, this is ultimately up to you. Some people feel comfortable with their arms by their sides or crossed over their chest, while others prefer to stretch them overhead. You can also put your arms on the support bars. Essentially, you should do whatever feels comfortable to you.

The most affordable Volkswagen ID. Polo Trend starts at just €24,995, or about $27,500, but you’ll have to wait close to two years to get one.

The new ID. Polo is “an affordable friend for everyday life,” as Volkswagen’s chief designer Andreas Mindt calls it.

After opening orders for the ID. Polo with the 52 kWh battery at the end of April, starting at 33,795 euros ($37,000), Volkswagen made good on its promise, launching the lower-priced, smaller-battery model in July.

The VW ID. Polo Trend with the 37 kWh battery went on sale in Europe in July, starting at just 24,995 euros, or about $27,500, with a WLTP range of 207 miles (334 km).

By mid-September, reports claimed Volkswagen’s entry-level EV was already essentially sold out across actross all trims, with more than 30,000 orders and a 10-month waitlist.

In a recent development, according to the latest enhancement from German automotive news outlet Edison Media, that number has doubled in about two months, and buyers now face delivery times of up to 21 months for the base ID. Polo Trend. Deliveries for the sporty GTI version are expected to be around seven months.

“We clearly planned too conservatively,” a VW manager told Edison during an interview. While VW expected about 90 to 95% to choose to lease, the leasing rate is only about 50%.

The larger 52 kWh battery version has also seen higher-than-expected demand, while 90% surprisingly opted to buy the optional €810 ($890) detachable towbar.

As a result, the tech giant is prioritizing higher-margin models, which is likely leading to longer delivery times for the base ID. Polo.

The entry-level variants “just clog up to the line,” Volkswagen’s manager said during the recent interview.

Demand for the ID. Cross, the electric equivalent to Volkswagen’s T-Cross, is also already exceeding expectations.

According to recent reports, the issue here is that the thing in sold out at 30,000 Units. it out to have production capacity beyond 100K!

Industry observers note that volkswagen opened orders for the entry-level ID. Cross Trend last month, starting at €27,995 ($31,000) in Germany, including VAT. The 52 kWh battery version will go on sale in the UK this week, starting at £30,260 ($40,000). The ID. Cross Life with the 37 kWh battery will go on sale in January 2027, starting at £26,985 ($35,500).

Volkswagen’s newly introduced entry-level electric cars are off to a promising start. The electric urban car family, which includes the ID. Polo, ID. Cross, and the CUPRA Raval and Skoda Epiq, has received nearly 150,000 orders combined since production began in June.

Sources indicate that however, the German automaker is still facing an uphill battle. The VW Group posted an operating loss of 5.9 billion euros ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter, its worst quarterly loss since the Dieselgate scandal.

In September, Volkswagen’s supervisory board approved its Future Plan 2030, which calls for reducing its global workforce by up to 100,000, closing plants, and narrowing its vehicle lineup to cut costs.

Recent findings suggest that the incident happened on November 9, 2026, on Arizona State Route 202 near Sky Harbor Boulevard in Tempe, Arizona. According to authorities, an AZDPS Highway Patrol State Trooper spotted the BMW traveling at a high rate of speed and passing other vehicles. Using a LIDAR device, the trooper reportedly recorded the vehicle traveling 170 mph in a posted 65-mph zone—an astonishing 105 mph over the limit.

Sources indicate that police were not going to engage in a pursuit at that speed, however, and said they decided to use the Highway Patrol Traffic Operations Center to track the vehicle's whereabouts. Eventually the BMW exited the highway, and police were then able to stop the car. At this time, the police reportedly noticed that the BMW didn’t have a license plate.

According to recent reports, police say the officer asked the driver how fast he thought he was going, and the man estimated his speed at approximately 110 to 115 mph. That's still far above the posted speed limit, but nowhere near the 170 mph that had him approaching Daytona 500 qualifying territory. The driver later claimed he hadn't realized just how fast he was traveling, according to authorities.

Why was he driving so fast? He reportedly told the trooper he was planning to trade in the BMW and wanted to take it for one last drive. Hopefully his latest car will be slower than the M2, because as police pointed out in their social media post, at 170 mph, the BMW was traveling approximately 250 feet every second. A crash at that speed would be devastating.

The driver was, unsurprisingly, arrested for reckless driving and endangerment, due to his excessive speed and unsafe driving behavior.

#109865. Can squirrels really survive any fall?

Can squirrels really survive any fall?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1126 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that on any ordinary day, you might witness the breathtaking display of squirrels high in the trees, doing what seems like effortless, daredevilish parkour.
  • A large, heavy human being attempting these same maneuvers would likely fall—and would be looking at a trip to the E.R., at best.
  • Industry observers note that yet squirrels, it seems, tend to walk away from these situations unscathed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that on any ordinary day, you might witness the breathtaking display of squirrels high in the trees, doing what seems like effortless, daredevilish parkour. They might launch themselves off one branch, bounce off another, and somehow reorient themselves in midair like it’s nothing.

A large, heavy human being attempting these same maneuvers would likely fall—and would be looking at a trip to the E.R., at best.

Industry observers note that yet squirrels, it seems, tend to walk away from these situations unscathed. You’ve probably even heard that squirrels can survive a fall from any height. But according to Dr. Nathaniel Hunt of the University of Nebraska at Omaha, this comes with an vital caveat: Even these brazen little gymnasts don’t stick the landing every single time.

In a recent development, “I would put an asterisk on the claim that squirrels can survive a fall from literally any height,” Hunt tells Popular Science. “Their size makes large falls surprisingly survivable, but they are not invulnerable.”.

It has been revealed that so, can squirrels survive, if not all, most falls? And if so, how?

It’s much more than luck that keeps squirrels landing safely; they are no more immune than we are to the laws of gravity. It’s what happens in the air—both in terms of their anatomical engineering and their instincts—that allows them to survive most falls and get right back to their nut-hiding hijinks.

According to Hunt, a falling squirrel faces three challenges: the speed of the fall, its orientation midair, and the impact when it lands. A squirrel’s small body helps; at about a pound, a squirrel weighs about as much as a loaf of bread.

Recent findings suggest that “Being small gives it a lot of aerodynamic area relative to its weight, so air resistance limits its speed,” Hunt says. “It also has much less kinetic energy than a larger animal.”.

So, squirrels’ light and small bodies help them hit the ground with less force, but that’s not all that’s going on. Hunt says squirrels instinctively know how to move through the air and land on the ground, which helps to optimize their already “favorable physics.” The tail is a key player in these midair maneuvers.

In a recent development, “The tail is more interesting than a fluffy parachute,” Hunt notes. “At low airspeeds, aerodynamic forces are small, but the squirrel can still use inertial tail movements to exchange angular momentum with the body and control orientation.” In other words, squirrels use their tail to control how and where they fall.

Sources indicate that research backs Hunt’s claim. A 2021 study found that squirrels experiencing unexpected falls were able to rapidly rotate their tails, a motion that caused the rest of their bodies to rotate in the opposite direction. Hunt compared the role of the tail to that of a “reaction wheel” on a spacecraft.

“Accelerating the tail in one direction helps rotate or stabilize the body in the other direction,” Hunt notes.

As a squirrel’s fall picks up speed, the tail may function more like the feathers on an arrow, Hunt suggests. If the squirrel starts to veer off course, the airflow pushes against the tail just enough to redirect its body into a stable position. Even then, the tail isn’t acting like a true parachute; instead of slowing the squirrel’s descent, the tail is nudging its body in the right direction.

According to recent reports, size, anatomy, and aerial reorientation are all key to a squirrel’s seemingly magical ability to survive most falls. However, there’s a third skill that plays an equally important part, one Hunt thinks may be “the most underappreciated part of the story.” Squirrels know how to come in for a landing.

It has been revealed that “A recent study I co-authored found that fox squirrels managed more than 80 percent of their landing energy through their forelimbs,” Hunt says of a study looking at squirrels leaping between branches. “They also adjusted their forces depending on whether they undershot or overshot the branch.”.

In other words, a landing isn’t just something that happens to a squirrel. On some level, they’re doing damage control.

“They are not simply hitting the branch,” Hunt notes. “They are actively controlling the collision.”.

So, how slowly does a squirrel have to fall to be able to walk away?

The answer lies in our furry friend’s terminal velocity, the top speed something reaches while falling once air resistance balances gravity’s pull and stops it from accelerating further. Hunt notes a squirrel’s terminal velocity can be reasonably estimated at about 20 to 40 mph, depending on its posture, limb position, and tail. For reference, Hunt estimates the terminal velocity of a cat—famous nine lives aside—at about 60 mph, while a belly-down human skydiver is likely to fall at about 120 mph.

“All of these are approximate, because posture matters enormously,” he states.

In a recent development, posture explains some of the variation, but size is ultimately the main driver. A giant squirrel, therefore, would likely fare much worse in a fall, even with perfect tail control and posture.

“You could not simply build a squirrel 10 times larger and expect it to tolerate the same fall,” Hunt notes.

According to recent reports, likewise, a squirrel’s comparatively slow terminal velocity doesn’t mean it’s out of the proverbial woods. It might seem that once a squirrel hits its maximum speed, height wouldn’t matter much, making a fall from 10 feet and a fall from 100 feet equally survivable. Hunt cautions against assumptions like this.

“Reaching terminal velocity does not make a squirrel immune to injury,” he states. “The landing surface, body orientation, and any collisions along the way still matter.”.

This complex interplay of physics, instinct, learning, and split-second decision-making is part of what makes squirrels a fascinating study subject for Hunt.

“What fascinates me is that you cannot neatly separate ‘the brain’ from ‘the mechanics,'” Hunt says. “Squirrel agility emerges from sensing, learning, body shape, and physical dynamics working together.”.

Sources indicate that there are many perks of being a Women’s Health style writer, and testing comfortable sneakers for work ranks very high on the list. My days are basically a rotation of steps—commutes, errands, long walks in the name of journalism—which means I’ve become extremely picky about what earns a spot on my feet. But time after time, I keep coming back to Hoka, aka the King of Cushion.

Since the brand debuted in 2009, Hoka has perfected the balance between support and comfort (the number one feature in a walking shoe), claims podiatrist Brad Schaeffer, DPM, foot surgeon and owner of Central Park Sole in New York City.

Sources indicate that hoka has not only asserted itself as a top contender in the sneaker scene, but the brand has also become a style statement, too, making ortho-looking shoes look cool with their plush cushioning. The brand churns out a bunch of styles for all sorts of activities, from running shoes to hiking boots, but Hoka’s walking shoes are some of my favorites. I get that combing through all the specs can get overwhelming, so luckily, I’ve done the legwork for you by testing and walking in Hoka sneaks for the past two years. Plus, I enlisted the help of Schaeffer and other WH editors to get the scoop on the right shoes for you.

After testing nearly every Hoka model, the Clifton 11 reigns supreme for walking. I was also a fan of the previous Clifton 10, and the newest version feels very similar. It is by far the most comfortable model in the series to date, and it’s earned a spot in my shoe rotation for its supportive yet flexible cushioning that gives me a spring in my step.

The first major difference I noticed is how light the Clifton 11 feels. Even after wearing it for several hours at a time, it doesn’t feel bulky or clunky. Which makes sense: Hoka did shave nearly half an ounce off the weight compared to the 10. The toe box is slightly more narrow, too, but I actually preferred the more secure fit because it kept my foot from sliding around without feeling cramped. If you like a little more wiggle room for your toes, I would suggest opting for the wide sizing, though.

Sources indicate that despite its lighter weight, it has an ample stack of foam padding throughout the midsole. That weightless yet cushiony feel makes it ideal for my longer walks throughout NYC. The shoe has a mild heel drop (the same as the previous model at 8 mm), which helps distribute pressure evenly across the foot.

I also found that the foam absorbed impact well on both pavement and the treadmill. My feet—unfortunately plagued by plantar fasciitis—never felt fatigued wearing this shoe. There's technically a rocker shape built into the sole, but it's subtle enough that I barely notice it—instead, my stride just felt smooth and natural whether I was walking or running. I’m also a fan of the durable rubber outsole that gives plenty of traction. I never feel like I’m going to slip while wearing these, even when walking down slippery subway stairs.

So far, the Clifton 11—which was debuted alongside the new Clifton Pro— does a great job of keeping my feet comfy and supported. It’s a great shoe for anyone in need of a comfortable, everyday walking sneaker that can also handle the occasional jog (unlike the Clifton Pro, which is geared more toward high-speed running).

Read more: Hoka Clifton 11 and Clifton Pro Review.

Technically, the Mach 7 is a running shoe—but don’t let that marketing label fool you. The previous iteration, the Mach 6, took home our 2025 Fitness Award for top walking shoe thanks to its blend of responsive cushioning, breathability, and lightweight construction—and the Mach 7 has built on that winning formula with an updated outer and grippier bottom. I’ve walked more than 150 miles in the ultra-light, ridiculously comfortable sneaker, and not once have I felt even a bit of foot fatigue or soreness.

In a recent development, the midsole is stiff yet flexible, while the cushioning is relatively low-key compared to its popular sibling, the Bondi 9. But, its slimness is an illusion. In fact, it’s just as supportive as most Hoka models and still offers a spring-like sensation after your foot hits the ground for a comfortable stride. This style doesn’t offer any special stability features for people whose feet tend to roll while walking, but I found it still does a decent job of keeping my feet in a neutral position, despite my high arches and tendency to underpronate (or land on the outer edge of my feet).

I wear the standard size and haven’t had any problems, but Accardi prefers the wide sizing, which she finds more suitable for her bunions and ability to spread her toes. If you have similar foot concerns or just like more wiggle room, we definitely recommend the wide fit.

While our one complaint with the Mach 6 was its lack of traction, I thankfully found that the Mach 7 features a more durable rubber at the heel and a stickier rubber up front, which makes a noticeable difference in grip.

Thanks to its incredible support and cushioning, the Gaviota 6 keeps my feet pain-free even after miles of wear. The shoe is designed with Hoka’s signature H-frame, which is a firm, dense foam in the midsole that provides a stable base to really lock your feet in place. I recently discovered that I have high arches, causing my ankles to roll inward when I walk, so this shoe has been a game-changer for me and my recent foot woes.

Industry observers note that while the Gaviota 6 is geared toward flat arches on paper, I’m currently contending with a bit of foot fatigue from my newly introduced 1-mile-per-day (at least!) running goal, and the Gaviota 6 has given my dogs the TLC they need. That’s likely due to the combo of plush cushioning and stability tech. After weeks in the Gaviota 6, my gait naturally shifted from a heel strike to a midfoot strike—exactly what Schaeffer recommends for pain-free walking.

Other super supportive sneakers I’ve tried tend to have a stiff midsole. Not so with this shoe. It has a hefty EVA foam for a plush feel, like I’m walking on marshmallows. Plus, I found this foam also does a bang-up job of absorbing impact from my strides. In other words, it’s super easy on my joints. Bonus points: its fabric doesn’t rub at all, even when I’m wearing thin socks, which is a must-have when I’m clocking hundreds of miles in it.Weighing in at under nine ounces, the Gaviota 6 actually sheds half an ounce from the already lightweight Gaviota 5. I love that it feels lighter than it looks, but it still has a bulky look that may not vibe with everyone. FWIW, I love the chunky aesthetic and wear it with hiking gear, wide-leg trousers, and even casual dresses.

It has been revealed that plantar fasciitis (that painful inflammation under your arch) demands serious support, and the Hoka Bondi 9 delivers. It’s the brand’s plushest model, with cushioning that feels soft yet springy like you’re walking on clouds.

Sources indicate that “I’ve been struggling with plantar fasciitis after months of half-marathon training, and this shoe—along with daily leg stretches—got me through long-haul walks pain-free,” says Accardi. That’s thanks to the Bondi’s plush underfoot cushioning and generous stack height. Schaeffer also recommends this shoe to his clients with plantar fasciitis, and says it provides a nice mix of cushion and stability. I also supinate and found that the Bondi 9’s premium foam midsole keeps my feet in a neutral position.

Contributor Lily Wohlner is also a mega-fan of this shoe. She's logged 15 miles walking in it and even wore it to the office to see how it holds up during long days on her feet. The verdict? It's the most comfortable shoe she owns, and she can wear it all day long without an ounce of foot pain.

Compared to the last iteration, this pair looks less bulky and feels lighter, and our style team found that this streamlined aesthetic plays nicer with most casual fits. However, be aware the shoe runs a tad narrow. Ritchey notes she doesn’t have particularly wide feet, but that the toe box is a bit too small. She walked over 17 miles in this shoe recently and started to blister slightly in her pinky toes.

“The Arahi 8 has become my absolute companion running and walking shoe ever since I started bouncing back from my stress fracture,” Accardi claims. “My podiatrist noted I needed something firm and supportive—too much squish and flex could cause my feet to roll and exacerbate my injury—and the Arahi delivered.” Don’t let the sturdy midsole fool you: It’s relatively comfy for a stability shoe, with just enough give to keep things feeling smooth. Compared to the Arahi 7, this version hugs the foot better and offers noticeably more bounce-back with every step. It’s got that sweet spot of stability and responsiveness.

Fitness editor Cori Ritchey is a huge fan of the shoe’s “well-balanced cushioning,” saying that it feels plush underfoot but didn’t affect her stability while walking long distances or running. She loves that the toe box on the Arahi 8 is a bit wider than the Bondi 9, giving her plenty of room to spread her toes. But, if you are into plush, cloud-like cushioning, you may want to stick with the Bondi’s. The Arahi doesn’t have that marshmallow-like softness—it’s much firmer.

One of its standout features is the integrated H-frame support system: Strategically placed firmer foam that wraps around the sides of your foot to guide your stride and keep your foot in a neutral position. You can definitely feel the structure working, but the payoff in stability is huge, especially if you’re recovering, need extra support, or just want something you can rely on to keep your form in check.

As someone who never reties her shoe laces (I always slip my sneakers on), the Hoka Transport originally caught my eye with its toggle lace system that eliminates the hassle of tying and untying.

It reminds me of my favorite Salomon XT-6 shoes and has a cool granola-girl vibe—which makes sense, since it is technically a hiking shoe. However, I will admit that while the Transport 2 looks very similar to the original, I prefer the sleeker look of the previous iteration. This version is also slightly heavier, but it’s barely noticeable while walking, and I chalk it up to the slight increase in cushioning.

Sources indicate that this shoe has quite a bit of cushion, but I found the midsole to be a bit on the stiffer side, meaning you just might want to plan for a longer break-in period before wearing it on long walks right off the bat. On the flip side, the firmness makes for a stable stride. It’s also great for neutral arches since it's not designed with any specific stability features in mind. But even with my slightly high arches, I felt locked in with every step.

According to recent reports, thanks to the high-traction, chunky outsole, I feel stable during trail walks across gravel, sandy paths, and uneven terrain. I also like that the outer shell material is Cordura, a water and abrasion-resistant mesh that’s built to prevent scuffs and withstand wear and tear.

Sources indicate that one thing to note: I went with the standard width, and the fit is a bit snug, especially with thicker socks. If you have wider feet, consider sizing up or opting for the wide version.

Hoka is known for its incredibly cushioned sneakers, but extreme cushioning is not always the best for keeping feet stable. In recent years, Hoka has leveled up their offering with more stability options, but the right pick depends on how your foot moves. If your stride is balanced, go for a neutral shoe like the Clifton or Bondi. These models provide cushioning and support without changing your natural gait.

Recent findings suggest that if your foot tends to roll inward (aka overpronation) or outwards (supination), a stability Hoka shoe like the Arahi or Gaviota features extra structure along the arch and heel to keep your feet aligned and locked in. This lowers your risk of aches and injury.

A popular Hoka sneaker, like the Bondi or Clifton, has super-thick cushioning made of EVA foam that is rubber-like and incredibly durable. With each step, it compresses and provides a snappy bounce. Despite the Hokas’ bulky look, they’re all relatively lightweight at under 10 ounces—hefty enough to keep your foot locked in, but light enough not to bog you down. Plus, several Hoka styles feature a "rocker bottom," which refers to a little lift under the heel and toe so those two parts of the shoe don’t touch the ground when standing still, similar to the base of a rocking chair. That shape helps you to walk from heel to toe, which means you exert less energy to propel your strides.

According to recent reports, some Hoka sneakers are designed for specific arch types: flat, neutral, and high. For example, the Gaviota is designed with flat feet in mind; the Clifton is designed for neutral arches; and the Bondi is suitable for high arches. If you’re unsure of your arch type, a simple test is to dip your foot into water and step onto a piece of paper. If you see your entire foot, it’s flat, while seeing half means it’s neutral. Seeing barely anything means you have a high arch.

It has been revealed that A heel-to-toe drop, sometimes called a midsole drop, is the difference in height between the heel and forefoot (toe area). Schaeffer states to look for a walking shoe with a heel-to-toe drop that puts your foot in a neutral position, which will be different for everyone’s unique foot and step pattern.

With their cloud-like cushioning, springy soles, and ample support, Hoka sneakers absorb impact from every step and keep feet locked in a neutral position. That makes them ideal for hot girl walks, a 12-3-30 walking workout, and taking your pup for a leisurely stroll.

According to recent reports, topping the list is the Hoka Clifton 11. I love the super supportive, plush midsole that keeps my feet from rolling and feels ultra-flexible. A close second is the Hoka Mach 7, our runner-up that’s technically a running shoe but totally crushes it for walking, too. It’s light, bouncy, and built for those who like to switch up their stride.

THE SECRET TO training your abs is out—and it entails more than situps and planks, more than just targeting your rectus abdominis, the ballyhooed band of muscle between your chest and your hips. If you want true core strength (and, yes, that six-pack), a growing group of experts will tell you that you need to carry heavy weights and walk. This forces your core to constantly microcorrect and rebalance as you move, explains Aaron Horschig, C.S.C.S., D.P.T., a St. Louis–based physical therapist. You also need to twist and turn, challenging your oblique muscles and back extensors.

“While there’s nothing wrong with training the abs for show, training for stability—which encompasses all of the muscles that surround the spine and hips—is essential training for everyone,” says Horschig. His new book, Rebuilding Milo, includes a variety of exercises, many of which challenge your entire core—think lower back extensors, glutes, and obliques, which all team up with your abs to stabilize and bolster your back, lending postural support.

Unlike body parts that handle just one or two tasks (like your biceps, which are most heavily utilized to bend your elbows), all those core muscles have a host of responsibilities. They work together to flex your spine (as happens during a classic situp), and they help rotate your shoulders so you can turn to look at a friend. They also prevent excessive rounding of the lower back (known as anti-flexion), a key tactic in the battle to stop back pain. The ideal abs regimen trains all these functions, protecting you against injuries and readying your core (and spine) for anything life can throw at you. Horschig states people finally get that. “More and more people are starting to understand the true role of core,” he says.

In a recent development, the end result of all this work? A lower back that’s armor-plated against persistent pain, and the ability to move athletically and fluidly. And along the way, you’ll build those six-pack abs, too.

HOW TO DO IT:An underrated plank upgrade, this move challenges your abs and obliques (and your glutes, too!). Start in pushup position, feet wide. Lift your left hand and touch it to your right shoulder. Keep your hips square as you do. Repeat on the other side.

REPS & SETS:Work for time, not reps, doing three 40-second sets.

HOW TO DO IT:Stand in a split stance, left shoulder next to the high pulley of a cable machine, both hands grasping the handle, then bend at the knees until your left thigh is nearly parallel to the floor. Keep your hips square to the front as you pull the cable across your body, then return it to the start.

REPS & SETS:Do 10 to 12 reps per side. Do 3 sets.

HOW TO DO IT:Stand holding kettlebells in both hands, the left bell at your chest, the right bell at your hip. Walk forward (or march in place) for 10 to 15 steps per leg. Move slowly, working to keep your hips square.

REPS & SETS:Do 2 sets per side, challenging your abs and lower-back muscles to keep you upright against the heavy load.

Sources indicate that TRAIN YOUR ABS EVERYDAY. Some muscle groups require several days to recover, but your core muscles are built to be resilient. That means you can train them nearly every day. Consider doing 3 or 4 sets of core work in every work- out, rotating in upcoming and different ab exercises to continually challenge your rectus abdominis, oblique muscles, and lower-back spinal erectors.

Industry observers note that NEVER GOING HEAVY. Bodyweight planks and situps are a solid starting point for your ab training. But just like any other muscle, core muscles are meant to be loaded and overloaded. Add resistance to your core training, and don’t be afraid to challenge yourself, especially on moves like the mixed-rack carry above. “You have to do that sometimes,” says the popular bodybuilder and trainer known as Ulisses Jr. “I’d be lying if I told you I didn’t load my abs.”.

Scientists created artificial, life-like muscles for humanoid robots

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (997 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, for better or worse, some scientists seem dead set on infusing humanoid robots with more lifelike qualities.
  • Industry observers note that designing robot muscles that act like the real thing poses some engineering challenges right off the bat.
  • “Soft robotic muscles need to be both strong and flexible to mimic human movements, but these properties are rarely found in the same material,” study co-author and University of Pennsylvania engineer Shu Yang mentioned in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for better or worse, some scientists seem dead set on infusing humanoid robots with more lifelike qualities. They’ve already experimented with stretching lab-grown human skin over robot faces and with a synthetic hydrogel skin that lets robots really “feel” burns and cuts. Now, a team of engineers at the University of Pennsylvania wants to dig under the skin. In a  study published this week in Advanced Functional Materials, the team describes a highly controllable artificial robot muscle inspired by the small muscles in human eyes and fingers. They put them to the test by having a robot hand strike piano keys at varying intensities and made a set of human eye muscles able to maintain a gaze. It all feels quite uncomfortably adjacent to the 1973 sci-fi film and HBO series Westworld.

Industry observers note that designing robot muscles that act like the real thing poses some engineering challenges right off the bat. For starters, most large robots today, especially humanoid ones, rely on bulky, rigid motors and components. That’s fine for more straightforward actions like walking and lifting, but recreating the muscles that move our eyes or fingers requires far more delicate precision. In this case, the engineers needed a material that prioritized flexibility and fine control while staying strong enough to hold up after repeated use. As with many aspects of robotics, tasks that seem quite easy for humans to do are actually often the most difficult tasks for machines. While bipedal robots have been pulling off dance routines and performing acrobatics worth of a Marvel superhero for years, they still fall flat when it comes to something as simple as folding laundry or holding a gaze.

“Soft robotic muscles need to be both strong and flexible to mimic human movements, but these properties are rarely found in the same material,” study co-author and University of Pennsylvania engineer Shu Yang mentioned in a statement.

According to recent reports, for their muscle fiber, the team settled on liquid crystal elastomers (LCE) combined with graphene and an embedded ultrathin copper coil. The LCE, a rubber-like material, acts as the actual muscle, both contracting and stretching. The graphene serves as a reinforcer, making the material both a bit softer and tougher, so it holds up even when opposing muscles pull in other directions. Together, these two ingredients can produce movement, but on their own they struggle to stay put. When heated, the LCE stretches but then keeps contracting, eventually creeping back toward its original length as it rapidly cools. That’s a problem for subtle movements like holding a gaze or pressing a piano key with light, steady force, where the muscle needs to hold a precise position over a period of time.

In a recent development, that’s where the coil comes in. The team added the coil inside the fiber to serve as a kind of temperature gauge, and the sensors determine when the muscle is losing heat and contracting. With those readings, the team could then gradually increase temperature to ensure the muscle held its position.

“We used the resistance of the embedded copper coil as a feedback signal and adjusted the heating power in real time to keep the resistance near a target value,” added study co-author and University of Pennsylvania Ph.D. student Xuelin Wu. “Because the coil served as both a heater and a sensor, we did not need a separate sensor for feedback.”.

With their artificial muscle designed, it was time to test it in real-world scenarios. First, the team fitted the muscles into a 3D-printed robot hand built to mimic finger movement. They then made the fingers press various piano keys at different levels of force and speed. Sensors placed on the bottom of the keys were able to tell how hard each note was played. The detached hand was no Mozart, but it worked.

Sources indicate that next, they mounted a pair of robotic eyeballs on freely rotating ball joints inside 3D-printed shells. The muscle fibers were attached around the edges of opposing pairs, which were meant to mimic how muscles in the eyes stretch and contract. In testing, the eyes shifted their gaze on demand, with controlled, repeatable movements. The resulting video demonstration is both impressive and unsettling.

In a recent development, the research joins a growing field of labs and companies racing to build artificial muscle systems. In 2025, Polish startup Clone Robotics took the idea to an extreme with a horrifying video of a faceless, human-sized robot dangling from a ceiling and writhing, its movements supposedly powered by synthetic muscles and a hydraulic system meant to mimic human muscles and blood vessels. They call  their creation the world’s first “musculoskeletal android.” Though it is likely that their video was more a shocking proof-of-concept than an actively working prototype, it nonetheless provides a glimpse into a potentially unsettling future where robots replace mechanical motors and actuators with more human-like muscle fibers.

It has been revealed that protoclone, the world's first bipedal, musculoskeletal android. pic.twitter.com/oIV1yaMSyE.

Recent findings suggest that the University of Pennsylvania researchers say the next step is combining more of these muscles into larger, integrated systems, where dozens of small muscles have to work together to produce more natural expressions. Down the line, they’re interested in potentially using AI computer vision to coordinate those into even more complex systems. Authenticity is the point. The long-term goal, they note, is to create robots that look and feel more and more like the real thing.

“I’m excited about the possibility of using this approach to create robots that move with the same subtlety and expressiveness we see in human faces,” concluded University of Pennsylvania engineer and paper co-author Ziyun Zhang.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Honda’s automatic engine start-stop feature is under upcoming federal scrutiny, after the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration received hundreds of complaints that engines failed to restart automatically from a complete stop at a traffic light on certain models, prompting the agency to commence an investigation.

The federal probe, announced on Friday, November 13, includes 1.03 million units of the 2024-2026 Honda Passport, Odyssey, Pilot, and Ridgeline. The inquiry also includes 2024-2026 Acura MDX units. NHTSA’s Office of Defects Investigation received 701 complaints related to the Auto Start/Stop feature.

Sources indicate that “To help improve fuel efficiency, the Auto Start/Stop system will automatically shut off the engine when a vehicle comes to a complete stop. The engine is intended to automatically restart when a driver releases the brake pedal. However, the complaints allege that the engines are failing to restart once they have been shut off by this system,” the investigation announcement reads.

It has been revealed that while automatic start-stop systems were created to improve fuel economy, Honda seems to be having a recurring problem with the feature. Federal safety regulators previously opened a probe into Honda’s automatic start-stop system in 2025. That investigation included 2.2 million late-model Honda Pilot, Odyssey, Passport, and Ridgeline models, as well as Acura MDX and TLX units. However, the new investigation includes 2026 model-year units. Inquiry documents allege that the two issue populations have different root causes and respond differently to repairs.

There have been no injuries related to this concern, according to the feds. EPA boss Lee Zeldin said the agency was investigating improvements or eliminating the technology last year; whether it sticks around in the long run, however, an engineering analysis of the stop-start system should bring Honda and NHTSA together to identify an effective solution to this recurring problem soon.

Sources indicate that A Fresh York transplant hailing from the Pacific Northwest, Emmet White has a passion for anything that goes: cars, bicycles, planes, and motorcycles. After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

“Of all the self-fulfilling prophecies in our culture the assumption that aging means decline and poor health is probably the deadliest.” --Marilyn Ferguson, author.

I was in an elevator with two preschool children in Halloween costumes, their parents, and an older couple.

The older man commented to the smiling children, “Oh, you are going to have fun on Halloween, I see.” The children and parents nodded at him in the affirmative.

It has been revealed that then he sighed and noted, “When you’re my age, you have a lot of aches and pains. Life is not as much fun when you get older.”.

Sources indicate that I was taken aback. So many negative stereotypes about aging in two short sentences, including the classic myth that old age is an inevitable process of decline and deterioration. I responded, “I don’t agree. I’m 82, and I’m enjoying life more than ever.”.

The man noted, “Well, I’m 73. You look very young for your age.” Was he implying that I was the exception that proved the rule?

According to recent reports, I’m not above fishing for compliments, but in this case, I was after something more notable—sending positive messages about aging to young children. I never realized I was going to need an “elevator message” to do it.

It has been revealed that usually, an “elevator message” refers to a business networking tool, consisting of one or two short sentences about who you are, what you do, and how your skills could benefit the listener, according to speaking coach Fred Miller. The idea of an elevator message is to convey the most important things about you during a short elevator ride. "Elevator messages" don't need to take place in actual elevators, of course. These messages can be employed at conferences, book signings, or even in the line at the coffee house. Writers, for example, can describe their background and latest book project; job-seekers can tout their most important accomplishments.

I had never previously considered that I might someday need an elevator message to combat stereotypes about aging. What I stated was simply a gut reaction to the situation. And the reason I am still mulling over what I said, and what I could have said, is because there was a life-and-death situation at stake. Well, not exactly, but here’s the research.

According to recent reports, psychology professor Becca Levy has researched the health and longevity effects of age beliefs. In one study, published in 2002, she and her colleagues followed 660 adults 50 and older and discovered that participants with a positive view of aging lived on average 7.5 years longer than participants with a negative view of aging.

Sources indicate that in her 2022 book, Breaking the Age Code, Levy cites other studies showing that people who held positive age beliefs scored 30% better on memory tests than those with negative age beliefs. She has also discovered that age stereotypes affect a surprising number of areas—for example, those with negative age beliefs had a slower gait, lower self-esteem, and exercised less. (For more details, check out this blog on how positive age beliefs can reduce dementia risk.).

Add to these results the amazing finding that most older people are happier people, as shown by numerous surveys. I was so shocked to learn the relationship between aging and happiness that I wrote a whole book (Silver Sparks) and numerous blogs about it. In addition, older people have good mental health, including a positive outlook on life. As researcher Laura Carstensen states: “People over the age of 65 have the most stable and optimistic outlook of all adults.”.

Of course, one negative comment in an elevator would be unlikely to mold the mentality of those young children. But I would suspect that a drumbeat of negative, ageist comments like the one I overheard could eventually have an effect on the mental outlook of those who hear them…which is everybody.

It has been revealed that young children and young adults are not the only ones who could benefit from an age-positive elevator message. A thoughtful message might also remind older people to challenge their own internalized ageism and recall the benefits of getting older.

Can we construct pithy elevator messages to replace the knee-jerk comments about ageism?

To jog your brain, consider these elevator messages about aging that are positive and accurate:.

What we say to children about aging will, of course, depend upon the age of the child and the situation.

With better messages about aging, we can help children face their future with optimism, possibly affecting their lifespan, healthspan, and mental health. And by voicing the positive truths about aging, we could also remind ourselves of the many advantages of growing older.

Here’s a challenge for you: What’s your idea for an elevator message about the benefits of growing older?

Thanks to my 11-year-old granddaughter Eloise for her ideas about elevator messages.

Tesla Cybercab has crashed 8 times, and the data shows a speed problem

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1181 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla’s Cybercab now has 8 crashes on file with NHTSA, barely two months after the purpose-built robotaxi started giving public rides in Austin.
  • Four happened in driverless “Robotaxi” service, and none topped 5 mph.
  • The data points at what we think is the biggest limitation of Tesla’s self-driving program right now: speed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla’s Cybercab now has 8 crashes on file with NHTSA, barely two months after the purpose-built robotaxi started giving public rides in Austin.

Four happened in driverless “Robotaxi” service, and none topped 5 mph. The other four happened with a test driver on board and Tesla’s driver-assist engaged, including one where a Cybercab hit a car at 53 mph on a highway in Philadelphia.

The data points at what we think is the biggest limitation of Tesla’s self-driving program right now: speed.

Tesla files Cybercab crashes under NHTSA’s Standing General Order in two separate datasets.

The first is the ADS (Automated Driving System) file, which covers Level 4 driverless operation. That’s the Robotaxi service, where nobody is in the driver’s seat. NHTSA’s latest ADS release, published this month, contains 43 unique Tesla reports, up from 22 in July. Four are Cybercabs:.

Industry observers note that those are minor. Two weren’t Tesla’s fault at all, and none involved an injury.

The second bucket is the Level 2 ADAS file, which covers driver-assist systems like Autopilot and “Full Self-Driving” (Supervised). Tesla has been testing Cybercabs fitted with steering wheels and a human behind them, often in places where it has no Robotaxi permit. Those crashes land in the ADAS file, with the driver type coded “In-Vehicle (Commercial / Test)” and the system “Verified Engaged.”.

There are four of them, all in September 2026:.

In a recent development, tesla redacted the narrative of all four as confidential business information, so there’s no way to tell from the public data who was at fault or what the system was doing. Pennsylvania State Police, Austin Police, Lehi Police, and Florida Highway Patrol are listed as the investigating agencies.

The Philadelphia crash is not the Broad Street crash where a Cybercab lost its door panel that we reported in October. That one happened on a city street in October. This one happened on a highway in September, at around 10 p.m. local time.

Industry observers note that tesla has no permit to run automated vehicles in Pennsylvania, and it doesn’t run Robotaxi in Utah either. In Utah, a Cybercab was photographed in Park City in September with a driver visible behind the wheel.

In a recent development, two of the eight Cybercab crashes involved injuries. Both are in the Level 2 file.

According to recent reports, across all 43 Tesla Robotaxi reports in the ADS file, the highest pre-crash speed is 29 mph. That was a driverless Model Y with two riders hitting a pothole in Dallas in September, after which one rider mentioned they sought medical care. The median speed across all 43 reports is 1 mph.

Industry observers note that not one of those 43 crashes happened on a highway. Tesla coded 21 on streets, 15 in parking lots, and 7 at intersections.

Those numbers say more about where Tesla lets the system drive than about the software itself. As we reported last month, Robotaxi sticks to low-speed routes inside small geofenced zones and largely stays off highways.

The Robotaxi Safety Report Tesla published on October 21 claims zero people injured by Robotaxi over 3,112,541 driverless miles between January 22 and October 18. It doesn’t mention the Cybercab’s test fleet, and it excludes every mile driven with a safety monitor on board.

Take the speed cap off and the picture changes.

It has been revealed that in the Level 2 data, Teslas with Autopilot or FSD engaged regularly crash at highway speeds. Our master dataset of Tesla’s ADAS reports holds 69 fatal crashes. Among the 52 where Tesla recorded a speed, the median was 53 mph, the same speed the Cybercab was going in Philadelphia, and 29 happened at 50 mph or more.

Today alone, we matched three fatal crashes to Tesla’s latest filings:.

Sources indicate that engagement within 30 seconds of a crash, which is what triggers these reports, doesn’t prove the system caused it. But the pattern is consistent. At low speeds in a tight geofence, Tesla’s crashes are scrapes with chains, curbs, and potholes. At highway speeds, they can kill.

Industry observers note that the Cybercab test fleet is where those two worlds overlap. It’s the same vehicle Tesla runs driverless in Austin, and the one Cybercab crash on record at real speed happened at 53 mph on a Philadelphia highway.

The Cybercab’s four driverless crashes are minor, and some weren’t Tesla’s fault. No one is denying that. But minor crashes still count, and so do the four Level 2 crashes that Tesla’s “zero injuries” framing leaves out. Both datasets describe the same vehicle running Tesla’s self-driving software.

It's looked to me for a while now that many of the improvements that people feel when they use FSD is not just the system getting better, but Elon pulling off the guardrails so the system attempts to do more stuff.

In a recent development, what the data shows is that Tesla has a speed problem. Its Robotaxi service looks clean largely because Tesla keeps it slow, off highways, and inside small zones. That’s also what makes it far less useful than a real ride-hailing service. You can’t take a Cybercab to the airport if the airport is on the other side of a freeway.

In a recent development, to be clear, we think Tesla is right to do it this way. Given what the Level 2 data reveals at 50+ mph, letting driverless Cybercabs onto highways today would be reckless.

In a recent development, but it means the hard part is still ahead. Highways, larger geofences, and higher speeds are where crashes become fatal, and that’s where Tesla needs its system to be nearly perfect before it can scale. The Cybercab’s test crashes suggest it isn’t there yet. The question is how long Tesla can keep growing a robotaxi network that can’t go fast.

As a longtime distance runner, my feet can get pretty roughed up after a grueling workout—even with the proper running shoes.
